Concentration name: African, African American, or Caribbean studies
description: The Africana Studies major is a liberal arts course of study that is at once a specific area of concentration and a body of knowledge that serves as a foundation for a variety of professions and fields of graduate study. Africana Studies majors have established careers in law, medicine, business, education, communications, politics, and the arts. Students are able to choose one of three concentrations: African, African American, or Caribbean studies.

The Agricultural Sciences major provides students with a broad-based foundation in the agricultural sciences, which will prepare them for a wide range of careers in production agriculture, as well as in allied industries. The major is designed to provide students with the flexibility to tailor their course of study to meet their individual interests, as well as to develop a deep and rich understanding of the science and art of agriculture. Students in the Agricultural Sciences major work closely with an academic advisor to design a program of study that helps them achieve their academic and professional goals. The curriculum is designed to prepare students for the challenges and opportunities in the agricultural sciences in the 21st century. Students interested in studying agriculture education should also select this major. Students completing the Agricultural Sciences major may also choose to earn a New York State provisional teaching certificate in agricultural education for grades K-12.

The American Studies Program provides a multidisciplinary approach to the study of the United States and the Americas. The program is committed to the study of race, ethnicity, and indigeneity; class, gender, and sexuality; and empire, colonialism, and globalization. American Studies is a field that brings a variety of disciplinary and theoretical perspectives to bear on the study of the multiple histories, cultures, and political economies of the Americas. The program encourages students to think capaciously and critically about what constitutes “America” as a historical, political, and cultural idea and how that idea has been contested and reimagined across time and from different social positions and locations. Drawing on the resources of the various departments in the humanities and social sciences, the program offers a wide range of courses. Students are required to take a two-course sequence, which serves as the intellectual core of the major. These courses are distinguished by their focus on theory and method and by their interdisciplinary approach. Majors work with an advisor to craft a coherent plan of study by selecting a concentration of at least six courses organized around a theme, a historical period, or an approach. The program encourages students to consider a semester in the Cornell in Washington Program. Courses in American Studies can be used to satisfy a number of college distribution requirements. For further information, students should consult the American Studies Program website or the American Studies Director of Undergraduate Studies.

The Animal Science curriculum provides a broad background in the biological and physical sciences and their application to the multi-faceted field of animal science. The curriculum provides a strong base for students with a wide variety of career interests, including veterinary medicine, livestock production, agribusiness, companion and service animal management, biomedical science, and conservation of endangered species. Qualified students have opportunities to participate in research projects with faculty members and may also compete for fellowships to conduct research during the summer.

Anthropology is the study of human diversity around the world. Anthropologists study cross-cultural differences and similarities in social institutions, cultural beliefs, and communicative practices. We examine the biological and biocultural origins of our species and the material remains of past societies. In our teaching and research we connect the humanities, the social sciences and the natural sciences. The anthropology major at Cornell provides students with a broad understanding of the discipline’s three subfields: sociocultural anthropology, anthropological archaeology, and biological anthropology. Sociocultural anthropologists explore the diversity of contemporary cultures and social institutions, from global corporations to religious movements. Anthropological archaeologists analyze the material remains of past societies to understand the development of social and cultural life over long periods of time. Biological anthropologists study the evolutionary history and biological variation of our species by analyzing fossils, primate relatives, and the human genome. Courses in the major address a wide range of topics, including: political and legal anthropology; medical anthropology; environmental anthropology; the anthropology of food and cuisine; human-animal relations; religion and ritual; race, gender and sexuality; and the ethnography and archaeology of various world regions (e.g., the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific). The major prepares students for graduate careers in anthropology and a variety of other fields, including law, medicine, public health, development, conservation, and education.

The undergraduate program in Applied Economics and Management (AEM) is a four-year course of study for students who want to have a positive impact on the world around them by applying a strong foundation in economics and management to a variety of complex challenges. It has an applied focus, which means students not only become strong analytical thinkers, they also learn how to use those skills to solve real-world problems. The AEM major offers a distinct advantage because it is based in both the AACSB-accredited Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management and the highly-esteemed College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS). This unique combination provides students with a strong foundation in economics and business, grounded in a real-world, problem-solving context. Through this approach, students learn to critically analyze complex situations and to implement effective, practical solutions.
Accreditation status: The Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management is accredited by the Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business (AACSB).

Concentration name: Art and Architecture, Material Culture Studies, Old World Archaeology, New World Archaeology, Skeletal Biology
description: The major in Archaeology is an interdisciplinary program that includes faculty from a variety of departments, including: Anthropology, Classics, History of Art, Landscape Architecture, and Near Eastern Studies. The major is administered by the Cornell Institute of Archaeology and Material Studies (CIAMS). Archaeology is the study of the past through material remains. Archaeologists study all of the past, from the origins of humankind to the present day. Archaeology students at Cornell may specialize in a geographic region (e.g., North America, Mesoamerica, South America, Europe, the Mediterranean, the Near East, Africa) and a time period, from prehistory to the recent past. They learn the methods and theories of archaeology, and about the modern practice of archaeology as a profession.

The Bachelor of Architecture (B.Arch.) is a five-year professional degree program that is structured to integrate a broad liberal arts education with a solid intellectual base in architecture. The curriculum is composed of a balanced sequence of courses in the areas of design, history-theory, technology, representation, and electives. At its core is the design studio, a place for inquiry, critical thinking, and experimentation. Design studios are complemented and supported by a robust curriculum of required and elective courses that provide a broad and deep understanding of the history and theory of architecture, technology and tectonics, landscape and urbanism, as well as representation and visual culture. The B.Arch. curriculum includes a significant number of free electives that enables students to pursue a minor or a concentration, to study abroad, or simply to explore the breadth of intellectual and cultural resources available at Cornell.
Accreditation status: The B.Arch. degree is accredited by the National Architectural Accrediting Board (NAAB), and the program is ranked as one of the top architecture programs in the United States.

description: The Department of Asian Studies offers a major in Asian Studies to students enrolled in the College of Arts and Sciences. The major is designed to develop a student’s command of an Asian language and to provide a broad-based understanding of a geographical or cultural area within Asia. The major can be pursued through two options: the general Asian Studies major or the more specialized concentration in China and Asia-Pacific Studies. The China and Asia-Pacific Studies (CAPS) concentration has its own separate admission and curricular requirements.

The Astronomy major is intended to provide a firm foundation in astronomy and astrophysics for students interested in a career in the field. The major requires a strong background in physics and mathematics. A research course (ASTRO 4940), an advanced course, a senior seminar (ASTRO 4490), and one additional advanced course are required. Majors are expected to attend the weekly undergraduate research and pizza seminar (ASTRO 4499) and the departmental colloquia (ASTRO 6990/ASTRO 7990). The major requirements are listed here, as well as on the departmental webpage.

The undergraduate program in Atmospheric Science provides students with a strong foundation in the fundamentals of meteorology and the option for in-depth study in a variety of other areas, including climate science, financial risk management, and environmental science. The major has a strong science base of physics and math as a foundation for the required courses in atmospheric dynamics, thermodynamics, and weather analysis and forecasting. In addition to the core atmospheric science courses, students are required to complete a specialization to provide more depth in their area of interest. Research opportunities are available with faculty in the department, and students may elect to write an honors thesis during their senior year. All majors have the opportunity to participate in the Cornell Chapter of the American Meteorological Society, the Cornell Weather forecast team, and the Northeast Regional Climate Center, all of which are housed in the department.

For students interested in a career in operational meteorology, this major satisfies the requirements of the American Meteorological Society for the Certified Broadcast Meteorologist designation and of the federal government for employment as a meteorologist. Opportunities for atmospheric science graduates include careers in weather forecasting, environmental consulting, the air quality sector, the energy and insurance industries, and a wide array of other private companies and government agencies. Many graduates also go on to graduate school to pursue more advanced studies and a career in research. Students majoring in atmospheric science can also complete a second major or a minor in a variety of other fields. Common choices include a second major in the College of Engineering or minors in business, climate change, computer science, and a senior thesis.

Concentration name: Sustainability for Food, Energy, and Water Systems
description: Biological engineering is at the interface of engineering and biology. It is a field that is based on the application of engineering principles to biological systems to solve problems in a wide variety of fields, from medicine to the environment. The Biological Engineering (B.S.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org, under the General Criteria and the Program Criteria for Biological and Similarly Named Engineering Programs. The biological engineering (BE) major is a demanding, multidisciplinary program for students who are strong in the physical sciences and who also have a keen interest in biology. The program provides a strong foundation in the engineering sciences, including thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, and transport phenomena. It also provides a strong foundation in basic biological sciences, including biochemistry, molecular biology, and microbiology. Building upon this, students learn to quantitatively analyze biological systems and to design and build instruments and processes to solve a wide array of societal problems. Biological engineering graduates are well prepared for careers in a wide array of fields, including medicine, biomedical engineering, environmental engineering, and biotechnology. Our graduates have also found employment in biotechnology, pharmaceutical, and food industries, as well as in environmental and biomedical consulting firms.
Accreditation status: The Biological Engineering (B.S.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org, under the General Criteria and the Program Criteria for Biological and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.

description: The biological sciences major offers a unified curriculum for undergraduates in the College of Arts and Sciences and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. The major is administered by the Office of Undergraduate Biology (OUB). The OUB, located in 216 Stimson Hall, is the primary source of information and advising for all students interested in the major. Students in each college are guided by a college-level faculty advisor in their respective college. The biological sciences major is one of the largest majors on campus. The faculty who participate in the major are from many Cornell colleges and departments. Students are exposed to the excitement and challenge of modern biological sciences while they pursue a curriculum that is tailored to their specific interests.

The biological sciences major is a new major jointly offered by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the College of Arts and Sciences. The major in biological sciences provides a unified curriculum for undergraduate students in the life sciences at Cornell. It is based on the conviction that a common core of knowledge and a common set of approaches are required for all life scientists. To this end, the major offers a curriculum that is both broad and deep, that can be flexibly tailored to a student’s interests, and provides an excellent preparation for graduate study, professional schools (in medicine, dentistry, and veterinary medicine), and for careers in many areas of biology. A key feature of the major is the requirement that students participate in an in-depth learning experience outside of the traditional classroom, including undergraduate research, study abroad, or an internship. The biological sciences major provides a rigorous and comprehensive education in the life sciences through its breadth requirements and thirteen concentrations.

Concentration name: The program requires students to organize their courses into a thematic concentration. Examples of thematic concentrations include: Environment, Health and disease, Law, policy, and ethics, Food, agriculture, and society.
description:
The Biology & Society major is intended for students who wish to combine the study of biology with exposure to perspectives from the social sciences and humanities on the social, political and ethical aspects of modern biology. The major is interdisciplinary and intercollegiate. It is offered by the Department of Science & Technology Studies in the College of Arts and Sciences and in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. The major is suitable for students who plan to enter careers in which an understanding of the biological sciences and of the social and ethical issues that they raise is of central importance, such as law, medicine, public health, public policy, business, and education.

Students in the Biology & Society major take courses in the biological sciences, as well as core and elective courses in the social sciences and humanities that examine the social, ethical, and policy dimensions of the life sciences. The major is designed to provide a broad understanding of biology, with the precise selection of biology courses tailored to the student’s interests.

The Biology & Society major is intended for students who wish to combine the study of biology with exposure to perspectives from the social sciences and humanities. The major is interdisciplinary and is sponsored by the departments of Biological Sciences and Science & Technology Studies. The Biology & Society major is designed for students with a strong interest in the life sciences who also wish to acquire a rich understanding of the social, ethical, and policy dimensions of modern biology. Students in the major will come to appreciate the nature of scientific knowledge and the ways in which science and society are interwoven. Many of the most critical issues of our time—food and population, biotechnology, health and disease, and the environment—are at the intersection of biology and society. The major is thus designed to provide students with the skills and perspectives to systematically confront these and other issues. Graduates have gone on to careers and graduate study in a wide range of fields, such as medicine, law, public health, public policy, environmental studies, and academia.

Biomedical engineering is a rapidly growing field that integrates the engineering sciences with biology and medicine. Biomedical engineers design medical devices, develop new therapies, and create diagnostic tools to improve human health. The undergraduate major in Biomedical Engineering (BME) at Cornell provides a strong foundation in the fundamentals of engineering, as well as the life sciences, and then integrates these to study human health. The BME major is designed to provide breadth and depth, allowing students to pursue a wide range of career paths in industry, research, medicine, and beyond.
Accreditation status: The B.S. degree in Biomedical Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org.

description: The Biometry and Statistics major provides a strong background in statistical and mathematical sciences, and it prepares students for careers in the theory and application of statistics and data science. The curriculum includes a core of statistics and mathematics courses, and it provides an opportunity to specialize by choosing an optional concentration in either Statistical Science or Statistical Genomics. Students acquire skills in statistical reasoning, data analysis and modeling, and computation. They also learn how to communicate the results of their analyses effectively. Graduates are qualified to pursue advanced degrees or to begin professional careers in a variety of fields.

Chemical engineering is involved in the chemical and physical processing of matter and energy that is the basis for our technological society. It is a broad and versatile discipline in which the chemical engineer may design, develop, or operate a process to produce a desired product. Chemical engineers lead the way in new developments in medicine, advanced materials, energy, and the environment. Students are well prepared for graduate study in chemical engineering or for a variety of other fields such as medicine, law, or business, as well as faculty advisers from the field.
Accreditation status: The B.S. in Chemical Engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

description: The Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree in Chemistry and Chemical Biology offers a flexible program for students who want to gain a solid background in chemistry while pursuing other interests. The B.A. degree is not accredited by the American Chemical Society. Students in the B.A. program must satisfy the College of Arts and Sciences distribution requirements. Students may also use the B.A. program as a basis for a double major. The chemistry part of the B.A. degree consists of a streamlined set of core courses plus an advanced course and a lab requirement. The program is described below.
Accreditation status: The B.A. degree is not accredited by the American Chemical Society.

description: The China and Asia-Pacific Studies (CAPS) major, based at Cornell and with a semester in Beijing and a semester in Washington, D.C., provides an opportunity for a select group of students to gain a sophisticated understanding of China and its relationship with the U.S. and the Asia-Pacific region. Students in the major gain a strong proficiency in Mandarin Chinese, take a wide array of courses on China’s history, politics, and society, get direct experience of the country, and develop an intellectual focus in a particular area of study. CAPS majors are part of a small cohort that develops close ties to one another and to faculty members affiliated with the program. The major also provides a structured framework for pursuing a rigorous and interdisciplinary study of China.

Civil engineering is the professional engineering discipline that deals with the design, construction, and maintenance of the physical and naturally built environment. This includes works such as bridges, roads, canals, dams, and buildings. It is a very broad field, composed of several very different sub-disciplines including: structural engineering, materials science, environmental engineering, water resources engineering, geotechnical engineering, and transportation engineering. At Cornell, these sub-disciplines are grouped into three primary areas: Civil Infrastructure (CI), Environment (ENV), and Transportation Systems Engineering (TSE). Students majoring in civil engineering select one of these three areas for primary concentration and another for a secondary concentration. The B.S. CEE degree is a professional degree that provides a basis for professional registration and practice. Civil engineers serve the public in a variety of ways: as municipal engineers; as consultants to architects and other engineers; as construction managers and contractors; as planners of urban and regional transportation and utility systems; and as managers of large public and private corporations. They may be involved with projects of all sizes and complexities, from the design of a small structure or drainage system to the planning of a regional transportation network or the management of a multinational corporation. The B.S. degree program in Civil Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.
Accreditation status: The B.S. degree program in Civil Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

Concentration name: Option I: Greek and Latin, Option II: Greek, Option III: Latin
description: The Classics major is designed to give students a thorough grounding in the fundamentals of Greek and Latin and to develop their skills in reading and interpreting the classical languages in their literary and historical contexts. Students will be expected to master the grammar and syntax of Greek and Latin and to become familiar with the major works of the classical authors. At the same time, because the study of the classical world requires a broad interdisciplinary approach, students are strongly encouraged to take courses in such related fields as ancient history, archaeology, ancient philosophy, and the history of art. The Classics Department offers majors in Classics, Classical Civilization, and Latin, and a minor in Classics.

Concentration name: Cognition and Perception, Language and Linguistics, Computation and Cognition, Neuroscience and Cognition, Culture and Cognition, Cognitive Science in Context
description: Cognitive science is the interdisciplinary study of the mind: what it is, how it works, and how it is implemented. The field includes researchers from psychology, linguistics, computer science, philosophy, neuroscience, and anthropology. Questions cognitive scientists ask include: What is the nature of belief and desire? How are memories stored and retrieved? What is the structure of human language? How do we see and hear? What is consciousness? How do we learn? Can machines be intelligent? What is the role of culture in shaping the mind?

The College Scholar Program offers a small number of students in the College of Arts and Sciences an opportunity to design their own interdisciplinary majors and courses of study. College Scholars design their majors in consultation with a faculty advisory committee of their own choosing. The Program is not an honors program in the conventional sense; it is an opportunity for students with a particular intellectual passion that cannot be pursued within a single traditional department to create a course of study that is uniquely their own. While each College Scholar’s program of study is unique, all Scholars are expected to pursue a course of study that is both rigorous and coherent. As part of their experience in the program, College Scholars participate in a regular seminar in which they present their own work and learn about the work of their peers. All College Scholars are required to complete a senior project, which is typically a written thesis.

The Communication major provides a liberal arts education that prepares students to be effective communicators. Students develop a comprehensive understanding of communication theory and research. They apply this knowledge to a variety of contexts—interpersonal, intercultural, organizational, political, and mediated—and learn how communication processes create, maintain, and transform individual and societal-level identities, institutions, and relationships. Students in the major select a focus area: Communication and Social Influence; Communication, Environment,Science, and Health; or an individually designed focus area.

Comparative Literature is the study of literature and culture across national, linguistic, and disciplinary boundaries. The Department of Comparative Literature at Cornell is one of the oldest and most distinguished in the country. It is renowned for its global and theoretical reach, with faculty specializing in a wide variety of literary traditions and critical approaches. The curriculum is unusually flexible and varied. Students design their own course of study in close consultation with their faculty adviser. Majors are encouraged to spend a semester or a year studying abroad, and often do so.

The Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) in computer science is offered by the College of Arts and Sciences. It is intended for students who are interested in the computer science field, but not in the comprehensive and intensive program required for a Bachelor of Science (B.S.). In terms of course requirements, this program is less structured than the B.S. program. The B.A. program gives students more opportunity to define their own interests and to combine the study of computing with a study of some other field. That other field might be a second major (e.g. music, economics), or it might be the application of computing in another field (e.g. computer graphics, computational biology, computational linguistics).

Concentration name: External Specialization, Digital Media, Artificial Intelligence, Foundations, Scientific Computing, Software Engineering, Systems and Networking
description: The computer science (CS) major gives students a thorough grounding in the fundamentals of computer science and a broad choice of advanced electives. Depending on the college, the CS major will earn either a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree from the College of Engineering or a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree from the College of Arts and Sciences. Both degree programs require a common set of core courses. The College of Engineering B.S. program has an additional set of college requirements, collectively referred to as the Common Curriculum.

The Department of Design and Environmental Analysis (D+EA) is dedicated to creating innovative, sustainable, and healthy environments through a multidisciplinary approach encompassing design, environmental psychology, ergonomics, and facility strategy and management. Our mission is to advance the field and to create a better world by engaging in research, teaching, and outreach that is both human-centered and systems-oriented. D+EA is a world leader in design research and education focused on how the built environment impacts human health and well-being. D+EA students learn how to think critically and creatively to address complex, real-world problems. They master the knowledge and skills needed for professional careers in which they plan, design, and manage residential and commercial environments.

The bachelor of arts (B.A.) in earth and atmospheric sciences provides a strong background in earth science, with a focus on breadth and a liberal arts education. It has a high degree of flexibility, offering students the opportunity for a broad education in the liberal arts and sciences. The B.A. degree is also appropriate for students planning to enter a profession such as law, business, or medicine, where a general science background is valuable. Students are also well-prepared for graduate study in earth and atmospheric sciences or related fields. Completion of the major requires introductory coursework in physics and chemistry, and proficiency in math through two semesters of calculus. Coursework within earth and atmospheric sciences covers a broad range of topics, including fundamentals in geological sciences, atmospheric sciences, and oceanography. Students select at least four intermediate- to upper-level courses from an extensive list of course options, thereby tailoring their major to their interests.

The Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences (EAS) is an interdisciplinary department with the common goal of advancing knowledge of Earth’s systems and their interactions, from the Earth’s core to its atmosphere and oceans. Our curriculum focuses on the past, present, and future of our planet, its life, and its climate, providing students with a firm foundation in the fundamentals of Earth science, while also emphasizing a systems approach to the study of the Earth.

The major in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences provides a flexible framework for students with a wide range of interests. All students learn about the fundamental physical, chemical, and biological processes that shape the Earth, including the formation of our planet and the solar system; the causes of earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain-building; the structure and circulation of the atmosphere and oceans; the history of life and climate; and the cycling of elements through the Earth’s interior, oceans, and atmosphere. After completing a set of core courses, students select one of six specialized concentrations described below, which allows them to explore their specific interests in greater depth.

The major is appropriate for students who intend to pursue a graduate degree and a research career in the Earth sciences; for those who wish to work in the fields of environmental consulting or management; for those interested in K-12 science education; or simply for those who want a broad-based liberal arts education in a fascinating field.

Economics is the study of how people make choices under conditions of scarcity, and the results of those choices for society. The subject includes the study of labor, land, and investment; of money, income, and production; and of taxes and government expenditures. Economists seek to measure well-being, to learn how it may increase over time, and to evaluate the public policies that affect it. As a major, economics is useful for careers in business, government, law and graduate study.

The Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) curriculum is a four-year program that provides a broad and strong foundation in ECE fundamentals. These fundamentals include circuits, electronics, computer logic, computer organization, and programming, as well as the underlying mathematics and physics. A rich and diverse set of ECE courses is offered at the upper levels in which students learn about and work on state-of-the-art devices, systems, and technologies.
Accreditation status: The B.S. degree in Electrical and Computer Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.

description: The Department of Engineering Physics offers a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in Engineering Physics. Engineering physics is the smallest of the engineering majors and is administered by the School of Applied and Engineering Physics. The undergraduate program in Engineering Physics is designed for students who want to build a strong and broad foundation in physics and mathematics and use that knowledge to solve modern technological problems. It is a demanding curriculum, but the rewards are great. Students in Engineering Physics take challenging courses from several different departments in both the College of Engineering and the College of Arts and Sciences. This gives our students a flavor for many different styles of learning and many different approaches to problem solving. Our students gain both a broad education in the fundamentals of physics and an in-depth understanding of engineering analysis and design. The program is flexible enough to allow students to prepare for a wide variety of careers. Our curriculum can be tailored to meet the needs of those students who want to continue their formal education in graduate school as well as those who want to enter industry directly after completing their undergraduate degree. We offer a structured curriculum, a friendly and supportive atmosphere for learning and a close interaction with the faculty. Our small size allows us to follow and respond to the specific needs of our students much more closely than larger departments. The B.S. degree in Engineering Physics is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.
Accreditation status: The B.S. degree in Engineering Physics is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.

Concentration name: Creative Writing, English and Theatre Cooperative Program, Honors, Law and Society, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) Studies, Minority, Indigenous, and Third World Studies (MITWS), Visual Studies
description: The English major at Cornell requires a combination of broad literary-historical coverage and a more specialized focus in a particular area of interest. Students must take at least eleven courses in the Department of English (or cross-listed with English) in addition to the First-Year Writing Seminars. Of these eleven courses, two must be at the 2000-level, and at least six must be at the 3000- or 4000-level. Four of the six upper-level courses must be taken in the Cornell English Department. All courses must be taken for a letter grade, and must receive a grade of C or better. Courses must be at least 3 credits. Advanced Placement credit does not count toward the major. Up to two courses offered by other departments at Cornell may be counted toward the major if they are approved by the student’s major advisor. Up to two of the eleven courses may be taken in creative writing. Courses used to fulfill the major must satisfy the following three specific requirements. (Note that one course may satisfy two requirements.) For details on these requirements, please consult the department’s website at english.cornell.edu.

Concentration name: Insect Molecular Biology, Systematics, and Ecology
Ecology and Evolutionary Biology of Insects
description: Entomology is the study of insects, which are the most abundant group of organisms on earth. The major in entomology is designed for students with a special interest in the study of insects and their relationships with people and the environment. As a professional field, entomology includes the study of insect biology and the application of that knowledge to the benefit of humanity. The curriculum provides a basic background in biological and environmental sciences with a special emphasis on the study of insects. Facilities include modern laboratories, an extensive insect collection, a library, and the Dyce Laboratory for Honey Bee Studies. Graduates are prepared for advanced studies in entomology and other biological sciences as well as for employment in various areas of the life sciences.

The Environment & Sustainability (E&S) major is a multidisciplinary, undergraduate program co-hosted by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the College of Arts and Sciences. The E&S major prepares students to address the significant environmental and sustainability challenges of the 21st Century. Students in the E&S major develop:

1) a fundamental understanding of the earth’s natural systems,

2) an appreciation for the social and economic context of environmental issues, and

3) the quantitative and qualitative skills needed for environmental problem-solving.

E&S majors benefit from the unique strengths and resources of two colleges, including world-class faculty in diverse environmental fields, research opportunities, and career advising networks. All E&S majors take a common set of core courses and then specialize in one of six concentrations to gain depth and focus in a particular area of environment and sustainability studies. The E&S major is administered by a cross-campus Program Board with oversight from both colleges. Students are subject to the graduation requirements of their home college and may enroll in the College of Arts and Sciences or the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

The Environment and Sustainability (E&S) major is for students who want to understand the complex system of social and natural interactions that shape our planet. They learn to evaluate the sustainability of human activities by considering social, economic and environmental impacts. The E&S major leads to a B.S. degree from either the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) or the College of Arts and Sciences (A&S). E&S majors apply to and enroll in one college, and follow the requirements of that college. Within the major, students select a concentration area that offers in-depth study in a particular aspect of environment and sustainability. Students from both colleges are part of one cohort of majors who share a set of core courses and a common experience.

Environmental engineering is the application of basic principles of science and engineering to improve the natural environment (air, water, and land resources) and to provide healthy water, air, and land for human habitation and for other organisms. Environmental engineers are involved in water and air pollution control, recycling, waste disposal, public health issues, and a knowledge of environmental engineering law. They also address global issues such as unsafe drinking water, climate change, and ozone depletion. Cornell’s undergraduate program is designed to provide a broad understanding of the technical, scientific, and managerial skills necessary for a career in environmental engineering. The curriculum builds on a strong foundation of mathematics, physics, and chemistry. Engineering science courses provide an understanding of fluid mechanics, thermodynamics, and transport phenomena, essential to quantitative description of environmental problems. The program also draws on the strengths of Cornell in biology and the earth sciences. A key element of the major is the design experience, which is incorporated into several courses and which culminates with a senior-year capstone design course. Graduates with a B.S. in environmental engineering can pursue a variety of career paths in industry, government, consulting, and nongovernmental organizations. The program also provides a solid background for students who intend to pursue graduate studies in environmental engineering or related fields, or in a professional field such as law, medicine, or business.
Accreditation status: The B.S. degree in Environmental Engineering is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

description: The Program in Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies offers students the opportunity to study a wide range of topics concerning gender and sexuality, grounded in the analysis of race, class, and ethnicity. Students will learn to think critically about how sex, gender, and sexuality are constructed and policed, and how they operate in both the past and the present, in the United States and across the globe. Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies courses offer an interdisciplinary perspective from which to analyze the formation of identities, practices, and institutions. Students pursue their own questions in an intellectually rigorous environment and in a supportive community of scholars. Courses in Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies may be used to fulfill a number of college distribution requirements. The program offers an undergraduate major and two minors: one in Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, and one in Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Studies.

The undergraduate program in fiber science and apparel design (FSAD) has a strong material and design foundation. The curriculum combines chemistry, physics, and math with design, art history, economics, and marketing. Students develop an understanding of the art of design, the science of fibers and fabrics, and the role of technology and merchandising in the apparel and textile industry. State-of-the-art computer-aided design, materials science and engineering, and textile testing laboratories allow students to have a hands-on learning experience. Students choose one of three options: Apparel Design, Fashion Design Management, or Fiber Science.

The bachelor of fine arts (B.F.A.) is a professional degree program that focuses on the development of the student as an artist. Students follow a structured curriculum in the creative and liberal arts and sciences. The program provides an opportunity for students to become disciplined in a particular studio practice while gaining a broad humanistic education. Students may choose to concentrate in drawing, painting, photography, print media, sculpture, electronic arts, or any combination thereof. The Department of Art is committed to the notion that the liberal arts and studio arts are intimately connected. The curriculum has been designed to allow a student to take full advantage of the resources of the university. Art majors spend about 60 percent of their time in art courses and the remaining 40 percent in academic subjects. B.F.A. candidates must complete 130 credits; 80 of the 130 credits must be in art courses.

Food science is an exciting multidisciplinary field that applies chemistry, microbiology, engineering, and nutrition to the development of new food products and the improvement of food safety, quality, and nutrition. The food science major is an excellent program for students interested in a career in the food industry, government, or academia. All students in the food science major gain a solid background in the basic sciences before taking a core of food science courses. The basic food science concentration provides a strong background for graduate study in food science or a related field. The food operations and management concentration is for students interested in business and the more applied aspects of the food industry. The food engineering concentration provides a strong background for students interested in the engineering aspects of the food industry or in graduate school in food engineering or a related engineering field.
Accreditation status: The food science major is approved by the Higher Education Committee of the Institute of Food Technologists (IFT).

description: The French major at Cornell is designed to give students a thorough grounding in the language and a familiarity with French and Francophone literature and culture. It is an appropriate course of study for students who want to go on to graduate school in French or other disciplines (e.g., comparative literature, art history, history, government, business), for those who want to prepare for careers in which a knowledge of French language and culture is a significant asset (e.g., international law, banking, business, or diplomacy), and for those who wish to combine the study of French with other disciplines (e.g., in a double major). Our courses develop and refine students’ language skills while introducing them to the history, politics, and cultures of France and the French-speaking world.

German Studies is an interdisciplinary program that includes the study of history, literature, film, philosophy, political science, music, and art. The major in German studies provides a broad humanistic education in the language, literature, and culture of the German-speaking countries. Students will develop their linguistic skills in German as a basis for further study, as well as their critical thinking and writing skills in English. Students may choose to focus their studies in German literature and culture, or they may want to complement their study of German with a focus on intellectual history or another national literature. Many German Studies majors combine their studies with a second major in another field such as government, history, economics, music, or engineering.

The Global and Public Health Sciences (GPHS) major, offered by the College of Human Ecology, provides a strong foundation in the life sciences and social sciences that prepares students for careers in public health. The interdisciplinary curriculum integrates a strong liberal arts education with a wide range of public health-related courses. Students interested in the pre-medical track should also consult with a pre-health advisor. Students interested in the program should contact dnsstudentservices@cornell.edu.

The major in government is designed to acquaint students with the theory and practice of politics at the local, state, national, and international levels. The department offers a wide array of courses, which are divided into four subfields: American politics, comparative politics, political theory, and international relations. The major is designed to be flexible so that students can construct a program of study that is tailored to their specific interests.

Concentration name: Geographic concentrations: Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, Middle East/North Africa, United States. Thematic concentrations: History of Capitalism, History of Science and Technology, Law and Society, Race and Empire, Women, Gender, and Sexuality
description: The history major is designed to be a versatile, flexible, liberal arts major. The program is designed to develop students’ analytical and writing skills, allowing them to explore specific historical interests and to acquire a broad understanding of the past and a sympathy with the people of other times and places.

The undergraduate major in the History of Architecture offers an opportunity to study the history of the built environment in a vibrant intellectual community. Our flexible curriculum allows students to work closely with faculty members on a wide range of topics, from ancient to modern. We explore not only buildings but also cities, landscapes, and other designed objects. Our courses examine the relationships between architecture and social, cultural, political, economic, and technological histories around the globe. This approach prepares our students for a variety of careers and graduate programs, including architecture, landscape architecture, city and regional planning, historic preservation, real estate, arts administration, law, business, and medicine.

The Nolan School of Hotel Administration is the world’s premier hospitality management school. The school’s mission is to create and disseminate knowledge about hospitality management through teaching, research, industry relations, and service. The school is an internationally recognized leader in the study of hospitality management, and its alumni are leaders and innovators in every facet of the global hospitality industry.

The hospitality industry is the largest in the world, and it is a dynamic and exciting industry in which to build a career. It includes a wide range of fields: hotel and resort operations, real estate and finance, food and beverage management, marketing, entrepreneurship, and much more. The Nolan School curriculum is comprehensive and provides students with a broad business education that is specifically focused on the hospitality industry.

The Human Biology, Health, and Society (HBHS) major provides a strong background in human biology, while preparing students to explore health issues from a social science perspective. The major is designed for students who are interested in careers in the health-care field, as physicians, dentists, veterinarians, or other health professionals, and for students who are interested in health policy, or a combination of these. Students will learn the basic biological sciences as well as the social and behavioral sciences that are relevant to human health. Students also learn how our social and physical environments can influence our health and well-being. This major integrates well with requirements for admission to most medical, dental and other health professional schools. With a strong grounding in biology, courses are available in human growth and development, anatomy, physiology, genetics, biochemistry, and nutrition. Complementary courses in the social sciences include human development, psychology, sociology and public health, which can lead to a rich understanding of human health in a social and ethical context.

Human Development majors explore the psychological, social, cultural, and biological development of people from conception through old age. The department’s five-area curriculum (Aging and Health; Cognitive Development; Human Developmental Behavioral Neuroscience; Law and Human Development; and Social and Personality Development) gives students a strong foundation in the behavioral sciences, while allowing them to pursue their specific interests. The major prepares students for a wide variety of careers in both the public and private sectors, including law, medicine, public health, social work, business, and education.

The School of Industrial and Labor Relations (ILR) is the world’s leading college of the applied social sciences focusing on work, employment, and labor policy issues in the U.S. and abroad. The ILR School’s undergraduate curriculum provides a strong foundation in the social sciences with a specific focus on the world of work. Drawing from the fields of economics, history, law, political science, psychology, and sociology, students learn to analyze and solve problems from a variety of perspectives. ILR’s flexible curriculum allows students to pursue a wide range of academic interests and professional goals.

Concentration name: Behavioral Science (BEH), Computational Social Science (CSS), Data Science (DATA), Digital Culture and Production (DCP), Ethics, Law, and Policy (ELP), Information Science and Technology (IST), Networks, Crowds, and Markets (NCM), UX Design (UX), Individualized Concentration (IND)
description:
Information Science (IS) is the study of how people and technology interact, and how technology can be used to address social, cultural, economic, and organizational issues. Information Science unites a variety of methods and theories from the social sciences, computer science, and humanities. It looks at system design as a human-centered, socially-aware process, using technology to solve problems in a wide variety of human contexts.

IS majors are leaders at the intersection of information, technology, and people. Majors develop a strong theoretical and methodological foundation in information science to become leaders in an information-rich world. The major has a strong technical core that is balanced with a focus on the social and cultural impact of technology. Students who major in information science have a passion to not only build the next great app but also to understand how the apps we use are changing us, our relationships, and our world.

Students who complete the major go on to a wide variety of careers, including user experience design, data science, product management, and software engineering at top technology companies such as Google, Meta, Apple, and Amazon. Others have started their own companies or become leaders in non-profits or the government. Many students go on to graduate school in a variety of fields, including information science, computer science, law, and business.

Concentration name: Data Science, Digital Culture and Production, Information Ethics, Law, and Policy, Information Science, Systems, and Technology, Interactive Technologies, Networks, Crowds, and Markets, User Experience, Behavioral Science
description: Information Science (IS) is the study of information and its role in the world. As an academic discipline, it is concerned with the processes of information creation, representation, organization, and retrieval, as well as the work information does in the social, cultural, economic, and political spheres. With its focus on computing and communication technologies, the field of IS has a strong design component: IS students learn how to build the systems that help us to create, manage and use information more effectively. The IS major is based in an interdisciplinary curriculum that combines computing and communication, social and cultural analysis, and design. Students take courses in three core areas: Content and Systems, Human and Social Systems, and Design. Students then choose an IS concentration and a set of electives based on their interests.

Concentration name: Digital Culture and Production, Data Science, Information Ethics, Law, and Policy, Interactive Technologies, Networks, Crowds, and Markets
description: Information is a critical resource in all fields, so understanding how it is created, processed, stored, and retrieved is essential in the 21st century. The Information Science, Systems, and Technology (ISST) major provides a strong foundation in the technical aspects of information and information systems, including the mathematical and theoretical foundations of information science, data structures, algorithms, programming, and systems analysis and design. In the advanced curriculum students explore topics such as machine learning, data mining, user-centered design and development, network science, data science, and information ethics and policy. This combination prepares ISST majors for a variety of challenging technology careers, while at the same time giving them a perspective on the societal and human implications of their work.

The Interdisciplinary Studies major, leading to a B.S. degree, provides an opportunity for students to formulate a program of study to meet educational and career goals not accommodated by other majors in the college. The program is developed by the student in consultation with a faculty advisor and is approved by the college’s Interdisciplinary Studies Program Committee. The program must be a coherent, integrated course of study that is both interdisciplinary and focused. It may not be a random assortment of courses.

The Italian major provides a course of study that is at once focused and flexible. Students majoring in Italian develop an excellent command of the Italian language and gain a deep knowledge of Italian literature and culture from the Middle Ages to the present. The major fosters skills in critical reading, thinking, and writing that are valuable in a wide variety of professions. The major consists of nine courses in Italian language, literature, and culture at the 2000 level and above. Of these nine courses, a minimum of five must be literature and culture courses at the 3000 level or above taught in Italian. Of these five courses, at least one must be dedicated to Dante, and at least one must focus on the medieval or early modern period (not including the Dante course), and at least one must focus on the modern or contemporary period. Courses taken to fulfill the major requirements must be taken for a letter grade and students must receive a grade of C or better. Courses must be chosen in consultation with the major advisor.

The B.S. in Landscape Architecture is a four-year design degree housed in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. This STEM-designated program is fully accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board (LAAB). In the U.S. and many other countries, you must graduate from a LAAB-accredited program to become a licensed landscape architect. The program’s core curriculum gives students a solid foundation in the skills necessary for professional practice and advanced studies. At the core of the curriculum is a sequence of eight design studios. Each studio focuses on a specific design topic and builds on previous studios. For example, topics include site grading and engineering, planting design, land use planning, design for climate change, and urban design. In each studio, students learn a variety of design processes, theories, and techniques. Studio instruction is complemented by a series of required courses in topics such as landscape history, plants and ecology, site construction and technologies, and visual representation. Professional practice courses prepare students for the contemporary workplace, and the curriculum is regularly updated to include the latest technologies used in the field. Beyond the core curriculum, students must choose a number of liberal arts courses, and they are encouraged to select a series of electives from landscape architecture and other disciplines at Cornell. By carefully selecting electives, students can develop a focus in areas such as ecological design, community design, urban design, or landscape art. To gain an expanded perspective on the landscape and its diverse cultural meanings, students are strongly encouraged to study abroad in their junior or senior year. In the Department of Landscape Architecture, the faculty are internationally recognized experts in their fields, including ecological design, urban design and place-making, community engagement, climate change adaptation, landscape history and theory, drawing and visual representation, and advanced digital technologies.
Accreditation status: This STEM-designated program is fully accredited by the Landscape Architecture Accreditation Board (LAAB).

description: Linguistics is the systematic study of human language. The linguistics major is concerned with the nature of human language, its function, structure, and history. Students learn how to analyze language and languages, from the level of sound to the level of sentence structure and discourse, through core courses in phonology, syntax, and semantics. Through the study of historical linguistics, they learn how languages change and evolve. Elective courses in linguistics provide students with opportunities to explore a range of topics including the study of meaning, computational linguistics, language acquisition, sociolinguistics, and psycholinguistics, as well as the study of specific languages or language families. Many students combine a major in linguistics with a major in another field, such as psychology, cognitive science, computer science, philosophy, anthropology, or the language-and-area studies programs.

Materials science and engineering (MSE) is an interdisciplinary field that applies the principles of basic sciences and engineering to the design and creation of new materials. Nearly every engineering discipline and all of modern technology is in some way dependent on materials. Materials scientists and engineers work on problems as diverse as designing stronger alloys for more fuel-efficient airplanes, creating new semiconductors for faster computer chips, developing new biocompatible materials for better medical implants, and creating new battery and fuel cell materials for a greener energy future. The MSE curriculum covers the fundamental science of materials as well as a broad range of engineering applications. Students have extensive opportunities to participate in research with world-renowned faculty in state-of-the-art facilities.
Accreditation status: The Materials Science and Engineering (B.S.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, https://www.abet.org, under the General Criteria and the Program Criteria for Materials, Metallurgical, Metallurgical and Materials, and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.

Concentration name: Standard Mathematics Major, Computer Science Concentration, Economics Concentration, Operations Research Concentration, Pure and Applied Mathematics Concentration
description: Mathematics is the language of modern science. It is a human endeavor that has spanned cultures and centuries. It is a way of thinking, a discipline of mind, and an art form. It is one of the great liberal arts, and it is a skill essential for a growing number of careers. Cornell’s mathematics program is recognized as one of the best in the world. The department’s undergraduate program is a lively and multi-faceted one that offers a large variety of courses and several different options within the major. Our students go on to be leaders in academia, business, government, and a wide array of other fields. The major is flexible enough to be compatible with the needs of students who want a deep and extensive training in mathematics and also with the needs of students who would like to combine the study of mathematics with a major or minor in another field. Many mathematics majors take a double major in another field, for example in computer science, biology, economics, and physics.

Mechanical engineering is one of the broadest of the engineering disciplines. It is concerned with the design, manufacture, and operation of a wide range of components, devices, and systems. Mechanical engineers are involved with energy conversion and fluid and thermal sciences; machine design, manufacturing, and control; and materials behavior and processing. The Sibley School curriculum is designed to provide a broad background in these areas and to offer a number of specializations. The undergraduate program is a preparation for a wide range of careers including industry, government, research, and graduate study. Mechanical engineers are employed in nearly every industry. These include major established industries such as aerospace, automotive, bio-medical devices, chemical, electronics, materials, and petroleum, as well as many emerging areas such as biotechnology, environmental engineering, nanotechnology, and sustainable energy. The Sibley School does not require students to declare a focus area, but most students will naturally gravitate to a few areas and many do undergraduate research or project work in these areas.
Accreditation status: The Mechanical Engineering (M.E.) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, www.abet.org.

description:
The B.A. in music is a liberal arts degree. It provides a thorough grounding in the discipline while allowing students flexibility to pursue a wide variety of other interests inside and outside music. Some B.A. students have a second major in another field. Many others have no other major, but take a wide variety of courses in other disciplines while concentrating in music. This degree is not primarily intended for those who wish to prepare for a career as a professional performer, although some graduates of this program do go on to such careers. Rather, the B.A. is for those who are passionate about music and wish it to be the focus of their undergraduate studies, but who are not yet sure what career they might wish to pursue after graduation. In this way, the B.A. keeps many options open.

Students contemplating graduate study in music are encouraged to study at least one foreign language (typically German or French) as part of their undergraduate curriculum. Students who wish to pursue the B.A. degree with a specific area of focus (composition, history, theory, or performance) should work closely with their advisors to select an appropriate combination of courses. Students who wish to focus on performance may, upon application and audition, be admitted to the B.A. degree with honors in music.

The major in Near Eastern studies is a liberal arts program that provides students with a broad knowledge of the cultures, languages, history, and religions of the Middle East from antiquity to the modern day. The department offers courses in Near Eastern archaeology, history, languages, literatures, and religions, as well as on a variety of special topics. A major in Near Eastern studies prepares students for careers in the U.S. government (the Foreign Service and other agencies), in journalism, in business in or relating to the Middle East, and in various non-governmental organizations. The major also provides an excellent basis for graduate study in the various disciplines of Middle Eastern studies. The department also offers minors in Near Eastern studies and in Jewish studies.

Concentration name:
Dietetics
Global and Public Health
Human Nutrition, Health, and Society
description: The Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in Nutritional Sciences degree program in the Division of Nutritional Sciences is a flexible and broad-based program that allows students to fulfill pre-health course requirements and explore the broad field of nutritional sciences from a basic biological science and/or social/behavioral science perspective. Graduates of the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences program are eligible for graduate study in a wide variety of fields, including biological sciences, nutritional sciences, medicine, dentistry, and other allied health fields, and other professional schools, such as public health, business, or law. Additionally, graduates are prepared for employment in health-related professions, in the food industry, and in community nutrition. The program is offered to students in both the College of Human Ecology (CHE) and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS). The information that follows pertains to students who are matriculated in the College of Human Ecology. Students interested in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences should reference the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences CALS page. Although the admission requirements differ between colleges, the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences curriculum is the same for all students, regardless of their college. Once matriculated, students may not transfer from one college to the other. Although the core curriculum is the same, each college has its own graduation requirements; the information on this page is for students for whom the B.S. in Nutritional Sciences is housed in the College of Human Ecology.
Accreditation status: The Didactic Program in Dietetics (DPD) at Cornell University is accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 120 South Riverside Plaza, Suite 2190, Chicago, IL 60606-6995, (312) 899-0040 ext. 5400. http://www.eatrightpro.org/ACEND. Effective January 1, 2024, the Commission on Dietetic Registration (CDR) will require a minimum of a master’s degree to be eligible to take the credentialing exam to become a registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN).

description: Operations Research and Engineering (ORE) is the engineering discipline that deals with the application of advanced analytical methods to help make better decisions. It is a diverse field that is also referred to as "the science of better". The ORE major at Cornell is designed to provide students with a strong foundation in the technical and mathematical tools of the discipline with an emphasis on their practical application in a variety of settings. Students learn and become proficient in the core skills of the discipline including mathematical modeling, optimization, probability, statistics, and simulation, as well as in the application areas of manufacturing, supply chain management, financial engineering, and data analytics. Students are encouraged to develop a concentration in a particular area of interest. The ORE major is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.
Accreditation status: The ORE major is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, http://www.abet.org.

Concentration name: Theatre and Performance; Cinema and Media Studies; Dance; customized concentration
description: The Department of Performing and Media Arts (PMA) is a community of artists and scholars who share a commitment to the arts as a vital component of intellectual and cultural life. We believe in the power of live performance and mediated art to stimulate the imagination, foster debate, and enrich our understanding of the world. Our mission is to educate a new generation of artists and scholars to think critically and creatively about the arts, to produce work that is both innovative and socially engaged, and to lead the way in a rapidly changing cultural landscape. The Department offers a diverse curriculum in theatre, performance studies, cinema and media studies, and dance that explores the arts from a variety of perspectives—historical, theoretical, and practical. We offer a major in Performing and Media Arts that leads to the B.A. degree as well as a minor in theatre, a minor in dance, and a minor in film. We also produce a full season of plays, dance concerts, and film screenings each year that provide opportunities for students to apply what they have learned in the classroom to the stage and screen. These productions are an integral part of our educational mission and a major contribution to the cultural life of the Cornell community.

Philosophy is the rational investigation of fundamental questions about the nature of reality, the mind, and the value. These questions are not the province of any of the special sciences; rather, they are the most general and abstract questions that can be asked. Philosophy is also the study of the methods of rational investigation of such questions, i.e. of the principles of logic and epistemology. And it is the study of the history of philosophical thought.

The philosophy curriculum at Cornell helps students to think, read, and write clearly and critically. The courses offer a broad and deep education in the liberal arts, and many of them have a strong interdisciplinary component, connecting philosophy with literature, history, law, mathematics, and the sciences. Philosophical study is excellent preparation for a wide variety of professional and business careers, including law, medicine, finance, journalism, education, and public service.

The Department of Physics offers a full range of university-level work in physics, from general education courses for nonscientists to doctoral-level independent research. The department’s goal is to provide students with a rich and varied education in physics and related subjects.

Physics is the study of the fundamental laws of nature. The beauty and mystery of these laws can be appreciated at many levels, from the most qualitative to the most quantitative. The department is committed to helping students with a wide range of interests and abilities to see the world from a physicist’s perspective.

A major in physics can prepare a student for a variety of careers. Some physics majors go on to graduate school in physics or a related field, leading to a career in research and/or teaching. Others go to professional school (law, medicine, and business are the most common). Still others go directly into the work force, in areas as diverse as computer programming, finance, and technical writing. The physics major provides an excellent general-purpose technical education.

The BA degree is a liberal arts degree. It is well suited for students who want a physics background for a career in another field such as medicine, law, or business, or for students who want to combine the study of physics with another discipline.

The Plant Sciences Major provides students with a fundamental and applied understanding of how plants work. Plants are at the foundation of all life on earth. They convert the sun’s energy into food and fiber, and they provide ecosystem services that clean our air and water. Plant scientists study plants at all levels of organization, from molecules to ecosystems, to understand how plants grow, reproduce, and interact with other organisms in a changing environment. This knowledge is used to sustainably produce food, fiber, and fuel for a growing world population and to conserve our natural ecosystems. Our majors are curious, problem-solving people with interests that range from social justice to conservation biology, from molecular biology to agroecology, and from improving human nutrition to increasing the aesthetic value of plants. Students choose to major in plant sciences because they will be able to make an impact in the world by addressing the grand challenges facing humanity, including food security, climate change, human health, and environmental stewardship.

The Policy Analysis and Management (PAM) major provides a multi-disciplinary, applied-social science education in public policy. PAM students develop a fundamental understanding of the policy process as well as the economic and sociological theories that can be used to analyze, design, and implement policies in the public, private and nonprofit sectors. PAM majors also learn the statistical and research methods that are needed to conduct rigorous policy analysis. The major prepares students to think critically about public policy and provides a strong foundation for a variety of careers and for graduate school. Many graduates enter law school or earn graduate degrees in public policy, health administration, or business. Those graduates who go directly to work are employed in a wide variety of settings in the public, nonprofit, and private sectors.

Psychology is the science of the mind and of behavior. The Psychology major is designed to provide students with a broad overview of the different approaches to the study of psychology. Within the major, we offer four different areas of study:

Perception, Cognition and Development (PCD): focuses on the fundamental aspects of the mind, including how we perceive and remember information, how we acquire and use language, and how our perceptual and cognitive abilities change throughout our lives.

Behavioral and Evolutionary Neuroscience (BEN): focuses on the biological basis of behavior, including the neural circuits responsible for our perceptions, memories, and actions, and how these systems have been shaped by evolutionary pressures.

Social and Personality Psychology (S&P): focuses on the psychology of everyday life, including why we are attracted to certain people, how we are influenced by groups, and how we form our attitudes and beliefs.

The courses offered by the department reflect the diversity of the field. They range from the study of the brain, to the study of the mind, to the study of individual and group behavior. The major is structured to ensure that students become familiar with the methods of psychological inquiry, as well as the different areas of the field.

The Religious Studies Program offers students the opportunity to study the religions of the world in a secular, academic setting. The program is interdisciplinary, drawing on the perspectives of the humanities and social sciences. Students in the program learn about the history, sacred texts, beliefs and practices of the world’s religions, and they also learn how to think critically about religion as a historical and cultural phenomenon. The curriculum is designed to be both broad and deep, allowing students to combine a general overview of the field with a more specialized focus on a particular religious tradition, a specific geographical area, or a critical theme in the study of religion.

Science and technology are defining features of modern societies, but their social and cultural significance is a matter of intense debate. Science and Technology Studies (STS) is a field that seeks to understand the social, political, and cultural dimensions of science and technology in the modern world. STS uses methods from a variety of disciplines, including history, sociology, philosophy, anthropology, and political science, to study how science and technology both shape and are shaped by their social contexts.

The STS major is designed for students who wish to pursue a liberal arts education in this field. Students in the major explore a variety of topics, such as the history of scientific discovery and technological innovation; the relationship between science, technology and public policy; the social and ethical implications of new technologies; and the role of science and technology in non-western societies.

Sociology is the study of social life, social change, and the social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations, and societies, and how people interact within these contexts. Since all human behavior is social, the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to the hostile mob; from organized crime to religious traditions; from the divisions of race, gender, and social class to the shared beliefs of a common culture. The undergraduate major in sociology provides students with a firm understanding of the discipline’s theories and methods and allows students to explore their own areas of interest in the discipline.

The Spanish major is designed to give students a thorough grounding in the language and a broad introduction to the literatures and cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. The major in Spanish provides an area of concentration for students who wish to specialize in the language, literature, and culture of the Spanish-speaking world. Satisfying the requirements for a major in Spanish can lead to a variety of careers in which a sound knowledge of the language and culture is a distinct advantage (e.g., international law, business, journalism, diplomacy, and education).

The undergraduate major in Statistical Science, which is available to students in the College of Arts and Sciences and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, provides a rigorous education in all aspects of statistics, from theoretical to applied. Students majoring in statistical science can take a broad range of courses, allowing them to not only be well-grounded in the fundamentals of the field but also to explore more advanced topics.

Students who complete the major in statistical science will have a wide range of career opportunities, including in banking and finance, the insurance industry, medical and pharmaceutical research, big tech and advertising, manufacturing, and government agencies, to name a few. In addition, students who graduate with a major in statistical science will be very well-prepared to enter a graduate program in statistics or a related field.
