The Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in Urban and Regional Studies (URS) is a pre-professional degree that prepares students to enter a master's degree program in city and regional planning. The curriculum for the B.S. degree is similar to the requirements of the first year of a master's program in city and regional planning. The B.S. degree combines a strong liberal arts base with a concentration in the theory and practice of urban and regional studies. A key feature of the degree is the multi-disciplinary approach to the study of urban areas and the planning process. Students have the opportunity to take classes in six different Cornell colleges, in addition to the core classes in CRP. Students complete a total of 120 credit hours to graduate.

The Viticulture and Enology (VE) major, offered by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, prepares students for a variety of careers in the grape and wine industry. The curriculum provides a strong background in the basic sciences, an extensive theoretical and practical background in viticulture and enology through a core series of courses, and the opportunity for students to specialize in one discipline. Students are prepared for careers in vineyard management, winemaking, business, and research and extension. The VE program is offered as a collaboration between Cornell University and our educational partner, Cornell AgriTech in Geneva, New York. Students spend most of their first two years on the Ithaca campus, and they must spend at least one semester at Cornell AgriTech in Geneva to complete required coursework.

The Department of Statistical Science and the Department of Mathematics jointly offer a minor in Actuarial Science for students who want to prepare for a career in the actuarial field. To be successful in this field, it is important to have a strong background in mathematics and statistics, as well as some knowledge of economics and finance. These subject areas are the foundations of the actuarial profession. Actuaries are experts in the management of uncertainty and risk. The primary function of an actuary is to determine the value of future financial obligations, such as the benefits provided by an insurance policy or pension plan. Doing this requires an in-depth understanding of not just the mathematics of probability and statistics, but also of finance and economics. By successfully completing the Actuarial Science minor, students will have the background to take and pass the first two professional examinations given by the Society of Actuaries (SOA) and the Casualty Actuarial Society (CAS). These are Exam P/1 (Probability) and Exam FM/2 (Financial Mathematics). Students will also be well-prepared to complete the SOA Validation by Educational Experience (VEE) requirements in Economics, Corporate Finance, and Applied Statistical Methods.

The Aerospace Engineering minor provides a formal structure for Cornell undergraduates who want to pursue a career in the aerospace industry or in a related research and development field. The curriculum provides a broad background in the scientific and engineering principles of aerospace engineering. Topics include fluid mechanics, aerodynamics, propulsion, structures, and dynamics and control.

The Africana Studies minor is intended for students who are interested in the study of the peoples of African descent in the United States, the Caribbean, Latin America, Europe and Africa. The curriculum of the minor is structured across three subfields within Africana Studies: African-American studies; continental African studies; and Caribbean/Latin American studies. The purpose of the minor is to provide a comprehensive, interdisciplinary, and focused study of the Africana experience.

The American Indian and Indigenous Studies Program (AIISP) offers a minor in American Indian and Indigenous Studies (AIIS). The minor provides an interdisciplinary framework for the study of the history, culture, and contemporary lives of Indigenous peoples of the Americas. The curriculum offers a rich mix of courses, which can be combined to create a course of study that is continental or hemispheric, and that can include a focus on a particular region, nation, or theme. The minor seeks to prepare students to work in a wide variety of fields both within and outside Indigenous communities. It offers a solid foundation for those students who may wish to pursue graduate work in the fields of American Indian and Indigenous studies, law, education, social work, cultural resource management, or other academic or professional fields.
Program name: American Indian and Indigenous Studies Minor

description: The American Sign Language (ASL)/Deaf Studies minor, offered through the Department of Linguistics, consists of 15 credits of course work. The minor provides a coherent program of study in the language and culture of the Deaf. The minor is meant for any undergraduate student at Cornell who has an interest in ASL, Deaf studies, Deaf culture, or a related area.

The American Studies Minor at Cornell provides a framework for students who want to develop their understanding of the complex texture of American culture, society and politics, past and present. The program serves students who are curious about the nation’s history, who want to make sense of the diversity of American experiences and who want to critically engage the meanings of “America.” Drawing on a wide range of courses and faculty from across the university, the minor encourages students to think across disciplinary boundaries to ask new and better questions about the United States, in all of its complexity and contradiction. American Studies students may focus on a particular historical period, a specific social group, a particular region, or a theme like law, social justice, performance, or visual culture. The program provides students with the critical and analytical tools to understand American identity, culture, and power in a global context.

The Animal Science minor is designed for students who have an interest in animal biology and the management of domestic animals. The curriculum provides a strong foundation in the basic sciences that are a prerequisite to many of the applied courses in animal science. A flexible curriculum, it allows for a diverse number of courses to be taken to fulfill requirements, which can serve the student with either a casual interest or a strong career goal in the animal sciences. The Department of Animal Science has more than 40 faculty members with a wide range of expertise, from molecular biology to farm management. Many of these faculty members are available to serve as advisors to students who select the minor.

The minor in Anthropology provides a structured yet flexible program for students to explore the field of anthropology alongside other intellectual interests. With its signature focus on cross-cultural comparison, the minor is an excellent complement to a range of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences. The minor helps students cultivate a critical perspective on their own society and an appreciation for the diversity of human worlds.

The Applied Economics Minor provides students with a systematic way of thinking about economic decisions that can be used in a wide variety of settings. The minor provides a framework for analyzing and understanding a broad range of economic issues, such as those related to management, marketing, finance, production, environment, and development. The tools and concepts learned are relevant to a broad range of real-world problems and situations as they relate to business, government, non-profits, and other settings.

The Applied Exercise Science (AES) minor is housed in the Division of Nutritional Sciences and provides students with a strong foundation in the anatomical, biomechanical, and physiological responses to exercise and physical activity. Students will have opportunities for hands-on learning in the Human Metabolic Research Unit’s Bod Pod and DEXA scan, teaching laboratories, and through applied research projects. The minor provides foundational knowledge for students interested in a variety of careers including physical therapy, occupational therapy, physician’s assistant, medicine, athletic training, and other allied health professions. It can also enhance the education of students with a general interest in health, fitness and athletic performance. The minor is a valuable complement to majors including nutritional sciences; human biology, health, and society; global and public health sciences; biological sciences; and human development, as it provides a unique focus on the application of scientific principles to human movement, exercise, and nutritional sciences.

The Applied Mathematics minor provides the student with a strong background in the techniques of applied mathematics. The prerequisites for the minor are MATH 1910, MATH 1920, MATH 2930, and MATH 2940, or their equivalents. Note that many courses in applied mathematics require some programming knowledge. The minor requires a total of six courses of three or more credits, chosen from approved course lists in two groups, as follows: 1) Three courses from Group A (3000-level), one of which must be an analysis course and one of which must be an algebra course; and 2) Three courses from Group B (4000-level), two of which must be a two-course sequence. The courses are listed under Center for Applied Mathematics. Substitutions for these courses may be approved by the Director of Undergraduate Studies.

The minor in Arabic provides students with a solid foundation in the Arabic language and introduces them to the cultures of the Arabic-speaking world. The minor consists of five courses, three of which must be at the 3000-level or above. Students must take one Arabic language course at the 3000 level or above. No more than one course may be taken in a related field and at the discretion of the Arabic program director. Of these five courses, at least three must be taken at Cornell. A grade of C or better is required for all courses to count toward the minor.

Archaeology is a quintessentially interdisciplinary field, drawing on the sciences, the social sciences, and the humanities to understand the human past. The Archaeology Minor offers a framework for constructing a coherent program of study in archaeology from the wide-ranging offerings of a number of different departments and programs. Students in the minor will achieve a solid grounding in archaeological method, theory and practice in their core courses, and then will build a particular specialization within a chosen area of emphasis.

The Department of Architecture in the College of Architecture, Art, and Planning offers a minor in architecture to undergraduate students in all colleges at Cornell. The minor provides a basic understanding of architecture and its relationship to the arts and sciences. The minor is not a pre-professional program of study and does not qualify students for admission to a graduate program in architecture. Students are admitted to the minor by the Department of Architecture.

The Artificial Intelligence (AI) minor is a new cross-college undergraduate minor that guides students in the study of the core principles of AI, as well as its ethical and social implications. Students will learn about foundational AI topics, such as machine learning, search, and knowledge representation, and also delve into AI subfields, such as natural language processing, vision, and robotics. The minor will culminate with a project course in which students will work on a substantial, team-based AI project. The minor is a joint program offered by the College of Arts and Sciences, the College of Engineering, and the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. The minor is administered by the Cornell Bowers CIS Department of Computer Science.

The Asian American Studies Program (AASP) is a university-wide program housed in the College of Arts & Sciences. Its mission is to advance the study of Asian Americans and to promote a fuller understanding of the lived experiences of Asian Americans in a comparative and global perspective. The minor in Asian American studies is open to all undergraduate students at Cornell University. The curriculum establishes a foundation in the history and cultures of Asian Americans, explores theories and practices of race and ethnicity in relation to U.S. national and transnational contexts, and engages with the complexities of Asian American experiences and identities. AASP courses highlight the histories, communities, and cultures of Asians in the Americas, looking at a range of topics including labor, migration, and refugees; law, politics, and policy; empire, war, and militarism; gender and sexuality; media, performance, and the arts; and social movements and community empowerment. Overall, the program emphasizes interdisciplinary and comparative approaches to the study of race, ethnicity, and diaspora, and views Asian American studies as a field of power, knowledge, and social justice.

The minor in Astrobiology is intended for students with an interest in the astronomical, planetary, and biological sciences. The interdisciplinary field of astrobiology is concerned with the distribution of life in the universe, a topic that has generated enormous public interest and is now a focus of a wide array of scientific endeavors, including NASA missions. The courses in this minor provide the basic astronomical and biological background for students interested in this field, introduce them to current topics of research, and expose them to the interdisciplinary nature of the field.

The minor in astronomy is offered for students who are not majoring in the physical sciences but who wish to have a substantive understanding of the fundamentals of astronomy and astrophysics. The minor may also be of interest to physical science majors who wish to supplement their major with a broad-based introduction to astronomy and astrophysics.

The Atmospheric Sciences minor is designed to provide students with a coherent and substantive background in atmospheric sciences. The minor is sufficiently flexible that students can tailor a course sequence that builds upon their own interests and the strengths of their major fields of study. The minor requires a minimum of 18 credits. Courses selected must form a coherent program and be approved by an advisor in atmospheric sciences.

The minor in Biological Engineering is intended for students in engineering or the life sciences who are interested in the application of engineering and quantitative principles to biological systems. The minor provides a coherent program of study in biological engineering, enabling students to choose a curriculum that complements their major and prepares them for graduate study in biomedical and biological engineering and related fields, or for professional careers at the interface of engineering and biology.

The Biological Sciences minor is available to any undergraduate in any college at Cornell who is not majoring in biological sciences. The minor provides a way for students with an interest in biology to gain a broad background in the subject and exposure to the new discoveries that are rapidly advancing the field. To complete the minor, students take a minimum of five courses in biological sciences including a two-semester introductory biology sequence, an organismal biology course, and at least two other courses in biological sciences at the 2000 level or above. The two upper-level courses must be a minimum of 3 credits each. Students who complete the minor have the equivalent of approximately one semester of study in biological sciences. Completion of the minor will be noted on the student’s transcript.

The undergraduate minor in Biomedical Engineering (BME) provides students with a strong foundation in the concentration areas of biomedical engineering. The BME minor is available to all undergraduates in the College of Engineering and in the Colleges of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Arts and Sciences, and Human Ecology. For students in the College of Engineering, the BME minor is intended to be completed in conjunction with an accredited major. The BME minor will introduce students to the multidisciplinary aspects of biomedical engineering research and the diversity of the biomedical engineering profession. Students are expected to have completed ENGRD 2202 and MATH 2940 as part of their major requirements before admission to the minor. A grade of C or better is required for all courses in the minor.

The Department of Statistical Science offers a minor in Biometry and Statistics. This minor is intended for students in the life sciences and provides a coherent program of study in the application of statistical and mathematical methods to the life sciences. The minor is administered by the Director of Undergraduate Studies of the Statistical Science department, who will approve a course of study for the student. The minor requires at least 18 credits.

The university-wide business minor (BUS) is for students in any Cornell college or school other than the Dyson School or the Nolan School. The primary objective is to provide students with a broad understanding of business and the U.S. and world economies. Students in this minor will take courses that will prepare them to be business leaders, managers, and entrepreneurs. Requirements include four core courses and one elective course. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C or better must be received to count towards the minor.

The Business Minor for Engineers (BME) is an interdisciplinary program offered by the School of Operations Research and Information Engineering (ORIE) and the Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management (AEM). The minor provides a solid foundation of business principles particularly well-suited for engineering students, preparing them for a wide range of career opportunities.

Students pursuing the BME develop a strong understanding of business fundamentals in accounting, finance, marketing, and management, along with key skills in leadership, communication, and business ethics. These skills and knowledge will complement your engineering degree, enabling you to excel in technology-focused businesses or in a variety of other business settings.

The BME minor is available to any student majoring in the College of Engineering. For more information, please visit the Business Minor for Engineers website.

The Caribbean Studies Minor is an interdisciplinary undergraduate minor that provides students with an integrated, multicultural, and hemispheric approach to the study of the Caribbean. It seeks to study the Caribbean as a region of diverse societies that have been shaped by and have made significant contributions to the broader world. The minor encourages an interdisciplinary approach to the study of the Caribbean and works to promote intellectual exchange and dialogue among students and faculty from different disciplinary and departmental units at Cornell.

The minor in China and Asia-Pacific Studies (CAPS) is designed for students in all colleges who wish to develop a sophisticated understanding of contemporary China and its role in the Asia-Pacific region and the world. The CAPS program emphasizes social sciences, including applied economics and management, business, development sociology, government, and sociology. As one of the preeminent centers for the study of Chinese language, literature, and culture in the United States, Cornell offers more than 100 courses on China. The CAPS minor offers an interdisciplinary curriculum designed to provide students with a structured yet flexible program to study China’s expanding global influence.

The minor in Civil Infrastructure provides a coherent program of study for students interested in the design and management of the constructed environment. Civil infrastructure systems are the foundation of modern society. They include transportation systems (e.g., highways, airports, ports); water resource systems (e.g., water supply, flood control, irrigation); environmental protection systems (e.g., wastewater treatment, solid waste management); energy systems (e.g., electric power, oil and gas); and constructed facilities (e.g., buildings, bridges, and tunnels). The design, construction, and operation of these systems involve a wide range of considerations including engineering analysis, materials science, systems engineering, economics, and public policy. The minor is flexible, and can be tailored to an individual student’s interests. Students completing the minor will have a greater understanding of the challenges associated with developing and managing civil infrastructure systems, and be better prepared for careers that require such knowledge.

The minor in Classical civilization is for students who wish to pursue an interest in the history, literature, and culture of the ancient Mediterranean world. The minor requires a minimum of five courses (totaling at least 15 credits) chosen from offerings in Classical civilization, Classical languages, archaeology, ancient history, ancient philosophy, and other related subjects approved by the director of undergraduate studies. Language courses at the 3000-level or above can also count toward the minor. The specific courses that will satisfy the requirements are to be chosen in consultation with the director of undergraduate studies.

The Department of Classics at Cornell is devoted to the interdisciplinary study of Greek and Roman antiquity. We consider this the original “area studies” program, embracing all aspects of the ancient Mediterranean world, including the Greek and Roman languages, but also literature, history, philosophy, art history, archaeology, and ancient thought more generally. We welcome students from across the university with a wide array of interests. Our students have diverse aspirations and go on to careers in many fields, including law, medicine, finance, journalism, education, and the arts, in addition to professional work in Classics.
The Classics minor is for students who want to become more familiar with the ancient world while developing their intellectual skills for careers in many fields. It has very flexible requirements so that students can focus their studies in areas that most interest them.
The minor provides an opportunity to read some of the world’s greatest literature in English translation; discover how Greek and Roman cultures contributed to the development of world civilizations; and explore the ways in which Classical antiquity continues to shape our cultural identities.

The Climate Change Minor is a cross-college, cross-campus undergraduate minor available to all Cornell undergraduates. The minor is designed to develop a broad understanding of the Earth’s climate system; the ecological, economic, and social impacts of climate change on people and the planet; and the ethical, social and policy dimensions for developing and implementing solutions. It provides opportunities for students to study climate change through a diverse and interdisciplinary curriculum that bridges the physical and social sciences, humanities, and arts. The minor is hosted by the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences in collaboration with the College of Arts & Sciences and the College of Engineering and administered by the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. Students can choose from more than 100 courses from over 30 departments in 7 colleges and schools to complete the minor. The Climate Change Minor requires at least 18 credits. Contact the Program Manager (climatechange@cornell.edu) for questions and help with planning the minor.

The Cognitive Science minor is designed for students who want to learn about the mind from an interdisciplinary perspective. The minor provides a framework for the integrated study of a variety of fields, including: psychology, computer science, linguistics, philosophy, neuroscience, and anthropology. Students must complete a core course in cognitive science and a set of five additional courses that provide a broad foundation in the various allied disciplines and a more focused study in a particular area of cognitive science.

The Communication minor is for students in any college at Cornell who are interested in the systematic study of human communication. The minor seeks to provide students with a strong foundation in communication theory and research, while also offering flexibility in the specific sub-areas in which they choose to specialize. Students who complete the minor will have a broad understanding of the communication discipline and will be able to apply communication theories and research to a wide range of social, political, and economic contexts. Students can apply to the Communication minor as early as their first semester of their sophomore year.

The minor in Community Food Systems (CFS) provides students with a strong foundation in the principles and practices of sustainable agriculture, and the economic, social, and political aspects of local food systems. The minor is designed to complement a number of majors in CALS and other colleges, and will prepare students for a diversity of careers related to food and agriculture, including farm and food business management, non-profit organizations, cooperative extension, and public policy. The CFS minor is administered by the SIPS Horticulture Section and is open to all Cornell undergraduates. It consists of a minimum of 16 credits.

The minor in Comparative Literature offers students a structured path into the discipline, its questions, and its methodologies. It is often a first step toward more advanced work in literature, theory, and cultural studies. It can be an excellent complement to a wide range of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and sciences. For students interested in the minor, please visit complit.cornell.edu or contact the Director of Undergraduate Studies, Professor Ewa Domańska (ed349@cornell.edu).

The Department of Computer Science offers a minor in computer science for students in any college at Cornell. The minor is designed for students who have a serious interest in the subject but do not have the time to complete a major. The requirements are designed to provide a firm grounding in the fundamentals of computer science.

The Creative Writing Minor offers undergraduates a structured opportunity to develop their craft and knowledge of literary expression. Students in the minor will work with a faculty advisor to develop a course of study that best suits their individual needs as writers and readers.

The Crime, Prisons, Education, and Justice minor (CPEJ) provides an opportunity for students to learn about the problems of crime, criminal justice, and mass incarceration in the United States, with an emphasis on the differing perspectives of social science, law, and the humanities. The CPEJ minor has two major goals. The first is to help students analyze the American criminal justice system in its historical and comparative context, and to examine its social, economic, and cultural determinants and effects. The second goal is to expose students to the educational and restorative practices that might help the criminal justice system better serve its multiple functions of promoting public safety, providing justice to victims, and rehabilitating those who have committed crimes. Students in the CPEJ minor will learn about the challenges our society faces in relation to crime and punishment, and also about the work being done on campus and around the country to improve the lives of those affected by crime and incarceration.
Program name: Crime, Prisons, Education, and Justice Minor

description: The Crop Management minor is an undergraduate minor administered through the Soil and Crop Sciences Section of the School of Integrative Plant Science. The minor provides a systematic program of study of the scientific principles and practices of crop management. The minor provides sufficient flexibility for students to focus their interests on a particular commodity group (e.g. food crops, forage crops, or turfgrass), or on a particular discipline (e.g. crop physiology and ecology, soil management, or integrated pest management). Students who complete the minor will have an excellent background for work in crop production and related industries, and for graduate school in an applied plant science. This minor is not available to students majoring in Plant Sciences, Agricultural Sciences with a crop production concentration, or students majoring in the Viticulture and Enology program through the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

The Dance minor offers students an opportunity to explore dance as a cultural and artistic practice. Course offerings in the dance minor give students a wide range of experiences, including dance technique, choreography, performance, and the historical and cultural study of dance forms. The curriculum is designed for students who wish to pursue a serious and comprehensive study of dance within the context of a liberal arts education. Students may focus their studies in the dance minor on particular areas of interest such as composition, performance, or cultural and historical studies. Students interested in the dance minor should contact the Director of Dance.

The Data Science in Astronomy Minor is an interdisciplinary minor offered by the Astronomy department for students in any Cornell college. This minor applies data science techniques to big data sets in astronomy. This minor is not open to students majoring in Statistical Science or students minoring in Statistical Science.

The Data Science (DS) minor is an undergraduate program available to students in all colleges at the Ithaca campus. Data Science is an expanding field that requires substantive expertise in an application domain and knowledge of computational, statistical, and mathematical data analysis. The DS minor will provide students with the key skills and knowledge for data-driven inquiry. Completion of the minor will be recorded on the student’s official transcript.

The Demography Minor provides undergraduates with a strong foundation in the concepts, methods, and substantive findings of population studies. Students learn how to analyze demographic data and understand how population processes are affected by and have consequences for social, economic, political, and cultural phenomena. The Demography Minor is available to all Cornell undergraduates. It is offered by the Cornell Population Center in conjunction with the Department of Global Development, and the Department of Policy Analysis and Management.

The minor in Design and Environmental Analysis (D+EA) provides students with a lens for understanding the complex interactions between people and their physical environments. Students in the minor will have the opportunity to develop skills in design thinking, human-centered design, and evidence-based design. The D+EA minor allows students to flexibly explore a range of D+EA content through three key areas: Design Innovation + Strategy, Sustainable Futures, and Health + Well-being. The D+EA minor is an excellent complement to a number of majors across campus including business, global and public health, policy analysis and management, communication, information science, computer science, engineering, architecture, and real estate.

The Design Innovation and Strategy minor provides a comprehensive curriculum that teaches the fundamental processes of design thinking, and the application of human-centered design to the development and launch of a commercially-viable new venture. The minor leverages the world-class education of the College of Human Ecology’s Design and Environmental Analysis Department, the Samuel Curtis Johnson College of Business, and the College of Engineering. It prepares students for a variety of roles in business, non-profits and entrepreneurial endeavors. Students will come away from the curriculum understanding human needs; how to create, develop and deliver products, services, and experiences to meet those needs; and how to strategically launch those products and services into the marketplace.

The Dyson Business Minor for Life Sciences (DBMLS) is geared toward students with a life sciences background who want to supplement their studies with a strong foundation in business management, and who are interested in a career in the life sciences industry.

The DBMLS is structured to provide students with a solid introduction to the language of business while emphasizing topics that are particularly relevant to the life sciences industry. Students complete five core business courses and one life sciences industry elective. The courses in the DBMLS are taught by Dyson faculty with extensive business experience and are offered online to accommodate students with demanding class and lab schedules.
Program name: Dyson Business Minor for Life Sciences

description: The minor in Earth and Atmospheric Sciences is for students who are interested in the fundamentals of how the Earth works, and who wish to have this recognized on their transcript. The emphasis is on the interdisciplinary nature of the subject and the interactions between the atmosphere, oceans, and solid earth. The minor is flexible enough to accommodate both students with a strong background in math and science and students with less quantitative preparation. The minor is especially appropriate for students in other science and engineering fields who want to broaden their knowledge of Earth systems, as well as for students who want a science concentration but are not majoring in a science or engineering discipline. The department has five areas of concentration: geology, atmospheric science, environmental geosciences, ocean sciences, and climate change.

The East Asian Studies minor is designed for students who are interested in East Asia and would like to build a basic foundation for understanding the region, but do not have the time to commit to the East Asia Studies major. The minor may be pursued along with any major in any college. The minor is a great way for STEM and other professional school students to pursue a passion in the humanities and social sciences while broadening their global perspectives. The requirements for the minor are structured for students to gain a breadth of knowledge through introductory courses and a depth of understanding through upper-level coursework.

The Education Minor provides a university-wide undergraduate minor that enables students from a variety of majors to study education from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Students in the minor will achieve an understanding of education as a complex and multidimensional institution, and of its central place in modern society. We offer courses with perspectives from across the campus, including those in developmental psychology, sociology, history, and policy analysis.

Students will demonstrate an ability to:

Recognize the breadth of factors that influence education and human development.
Examine educational theory and practice from multiple disciplinary perspectives.
Critically analyze educational policy and practice.
Appreciate the importance of inquiry and reflection in promoting effective teaching and learning.
Communicate effectively in a variety of contexts.

The Electrical and Computer Engineering (ECE) minor is available to all undergraduates in the College of Engineering, and to students in other colleges who are majoring in a technical field. The ECE minor is particularly appropriate for students in other engineering majors who wish to broaden their horizons, for students in other technical fields (such as physics, mathematics, and computer science) who want to learn about the engineering applications of their science, and for students who are simply interested in the exciting field of ECE. The ECE minor curriculum is designed to provide a general overview of the field, so it is flexible. Students may choose courses in a number of areas of ECE or may concentrate on one or two. There are three components to the ECE minor: ECE foundation courses, ECE core courses, and ECE electives. These must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C or better must be received.

The Engineering Communications Program (ECP) offers a minor in engineering communications. The minor is designed for students who are interested in developing their communication skills. The minor helps students to learn how to communicate effectively about engineering and technical subjects to a wide range of audiences, from the general public to professional engineers. Students in the minor will also learn to work more effectively in teams and to take on leadership roles.

The Engineering Entrepreneurship minor, open to all undergraduate students in the College of Engineering, provides students an opportunity to build on their technical education with a structured curriculum to better understand the process of technology-based entrepreneurship. Many engineering students are interested in starting companies, or joining start-ups, upon graduation. The minor will help students develop business and entrepreneurial skills to translate technical inventions into commercial ventures. Students will learn the process of evaluating the commercial potential of a technology, developing a business plan and launching a new company.

The Engineering Management Minor is a new minor in the College of Engineering that may be of particular interest to students in the College of Engineering and other Cornell colleges who want to combine their primary technical discipline with a set of courses designed to provide them with the management and leadership skills needed for their careers. A key goal of the minor is to develop leaders for a technical world. In an effort to keep the minor as accessible to as many students as possible, it has been designed to satisfy requirements for other minors and majors, where possible.

The English minor offers undergraduates the opportunity to study and practice the arts of literary interpretation and writing. Students who minor in English learn about a wide variety of literatures in English, their historical and cultural contexts, and the critical methods by which they can be understood. They work closely with a renowned faculty to develop their own critical and analytical voices and to hone their skills as writers.

The minor in Entomology provides a strong background in the science of entomology and a broader appreciation of the fascinating and important roles that insects play in the earth’s ecosystems. A minor in Entomology can prepare students for a diversity of career paths, including pest management, conservation and environmental biology, toxicology, apiculture, and human or veterinary medicine.

The cross-campus undergraduate Minor in Entrepreneurship and Innovation provides students in any major with the opportunity to study the vital processes of entrepreneurship and innovation, complementing the academic content of their majors and adding a dimension of practice to their university education. The goal of the minor is to provide students with the knowledge and skills to become entrepreneurs or ‘intrapreneurs’ (innovators within large organizations). The minor requires a sequence of courses and a significant team-based experience focused on the development of an innovative product, service or venture.

Concentration name: Environmental Biology & Applied Ecology, Environmental & Resource Economics, Environmental Humanities, Environmental Policy & Governance, Land, Air & Water Resources, Sustainable Food & Agricultural Systems
description: The environment and sustainability (E&S) minor is an opportunity for undergraduate students from any college at Cornell to develop a transdisciplinary understanding of environmental and sustainability issues. The minor is structured to help students become literate and critical thinkers with respect to the complex interplay between human and natural systems. Through a core course, a set of distribution requirements, an area of concentration in a specific subject area, and a capstone experience, students are challenged to integrate different disciplinary approaches to address a range of pressing environmental and sustainability challenges. The minor is designed to be accessible to all students, regardless of their major, and to provide opportunities to engage with world-class faculty from across the university who share a common interest in the environment and sustainability. Students who complete the minor will have a credential that demonstrates their commitment to and knowledge of environment and sustainability.

The Environmental Engineering Minor provides an opportunity for all Cornell undergraduates to learn about the scientific, engineering, and economic foundations of environmental engineering and to apply that knowledge to current environmental challenges. The minor has a flexible structure that allows students to select courses in one or more focus areas of interest, including environmental processes, environmental systems, and sustainable energy systems.

The minor in European studies, offered by the Institute for European Studies (IES) as part of the Mario Einaudi Center for International Studies, provides a coherent structure for students with an interest in the languages, cultures, and societies of Europe.

The minor is designed for students in any of Cornell’s undergraduate colleges who have a special interest in European studies. The minor helps students to craft a coherent program of study of Europe from the existing university curriculum. Students pursuing the minor will work with a member of the European studies faculty in their college to design a curriculum that is appropriate to their interests and major field of study. Upon graduating, students will have the European studies minor designated on their official transcript.

The undergraduate minor in Fashion Studies offers students a multi-disciplinary approach to study the history, material culture, design and contemporary business of fashion. Students will complete a required foundation course, FSAD 1140 - Introduction to Fashion Design, as well as a selection of courses from a pre-approved list spanning across art, anthropology, design, economics, fiber science, history, management and sociology. The minor is offered to all undergraduate students in all colleges. It is administered by the Department of Fiber Science and Apparel Design. Students must apply to be in the minor, ideally by the first semester of their junior year. Students are responsible for fulfilling all prerequisites for the listed courses. Students are also responsible for determining if the courses selected for the minor may be used to fulfill college/major requirements. Admission to the minor requires a minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0. Interested students must meet with an FSAD advisor to be accepted into the minor. It is important to meet with the advisor early in academic career to plan the program of study and ensure all requirements can be met. Students must complete a minimum of 18 credits for the minor.

The FGSS minor offers students an interdisciplinary opportunity to study gender and sexuality. The minor provides a broad overview of the study of gender and sexuality as well as an opportunity to focus on a particular area of interest. Coursework in FGSS is grounded in the humanities and social sciences and draws from other fields as well, including the visual arts, biological sciences, and law. Students who minor in FGSS take a total of five courses. At least one of these five courses must be at the 3000-level or higher. Students are encouraged to choose a course of study that reflects their own interests, in consultation with the Director of Undergraduate Studies. All courses must be passed with a letter grade of C or better. Only courses listed in the FGSS course offerings may be used for the minor, unless an exception is granted by the Director of Undergraduate Studies. The S/U option is not available for any course that is to be counted toward the minor. A maximum of two courses from a student’s major may be used for the FGSS minor. All courses used for the minor must be taken for a letter grade. We do not accept study abroad credits, transfer credits, or First-Year Writing Seminars as part of the minor.

The Fiber Science minor offers students an opportunity to study the physical, chemical, and engineering properties of fibrous materials and their applications, which range from advanced engineering composites, to biomedical implants and fabrics for protective clothing. Through a sequence of core courses, students will gain a fundamental understanding of polymers, fibers, and the chemistry and physics of materials. Technical electives will offer students the opportunity to gain breadth in engineering, chemistry, and the applied sciences.

The film minor offers undergraduates an interdisciplinary curriculum in the history, theory, and criticism of film and other moving-image media. Students who complete the minor will gain a critical and historical understanding of the cinematic medium, including its relationship to culture, society, and other art forms. They will also learn a variety of analytical and interpretive skills for the study of film. The minor provides a strong complement to majors in the humanities and social sciences.

The film minor is administered by the Department of Performing and Media Arts.

The Department of Art offers a minor in fine arts. The minor in fine arts provides students with a strong foundation in the practice, history, and theory of art. Students must be on track to complete at least 18 credits with a grade of C or better to complete the minor.

The Food and Agricultural Business minor provides students with core business management and marketing principles, and an understanding of the structure and institutions of the food and agricultural sectors of the economy. It is intended for students who are interested in careers in the food and agricultural industries, from production agriculture through food processing and distribution. Students from a wide variety of majors find this minor a valuable complement to their studies. The minor requires 18 credits, including 6 credits of core courses and at least 12 credits of business management and marketing electives. Many of the business management and marketing electives have prerequisites that are part of the core requirements.

The Food Science minor is available to all Cornell undergraduate students. This minor is not available to Food Science majors. The minor provides students with a substantive understanding of the scientific principles involved in food processing, preservation, and safety. This is accomplished through a defined set of core food science courses that include food chemistry, food engineering, food microbiology, food safety, and sensory evaluation. Students are then able to select from a diverse set of elective courses to focus on areas of specific interest. Examples include dairy science, food fermentations, food quality, food law, food product development, and nutrition.

The minor in French offers students the opportunity to combine an interest in French and francophone language, literature, and culture with their major in another field. Courses for the minor taken in the Department of Romance Studies must be taught in French. No more than one course may be taken with a non-Cornell program abroad. No more than two courses may be taken at another institution (including Cornell- or non-Cornell-sponsored programs abroad).

The French minor consists of five courses (of at least 3 credits) in French language, literature, or culture at the 2000 level or above. No more than two courses at the 2000 level can be counted toward the minor. Of the five courses, at least three must be taken at Cornell. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and completed with a grade of C or better. AP credit may not be used to fulfill the requirements of the minor.

The Fungal Biology Minor is intended for students who have an interest in fungi and their roles in the environment, in causing plant and animal diseases, and in industrial applications. Students will develop a basic knowledge of fungi and will supplement this with courses in a selected area of specialization. Through this minor, students will have an opportunity to interact with the more than twenty-five faculty at Cornell University with whom they have common interests.

The undergraduate minor in Game Design is for students who are interested in the design, development, and study of games. The minor is highly interdisciplinary and provides students with a broad understanding of the field, as well as an opportunity to focus on a particular area of interest. The Game Design Initiative at Cornell is a collaboration of faculty from the College of Arts & Sciences, the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, the College of Engineering, and the College of Architecture, Art, and Planning. The program is administered by the Game Design Initiative in the Department of Computer Science.

The German Studies minor is designed for students who are interested in developing a fuller understanding of the culture of the German-speaking world. The minor provides a structure for students from all colleges and majors to develop a course of study that combines the acquisition of German language skills with the study of German literature, culture, history, and politics. Recent minors have combined their work in German Studies with majors in a wide range of fields from across the university: chemistry, biology, physics, government, history, music, hotel administration, industrial and labor relations, etc.

The Gerontology Minor provides a multidisciplinary approach to the study of the aging process and the life course. Gerontology draws on research from all the social and behavioral sciences, the biological sciences, and the humanities. Courses provide a broad understanding of the field and permit students to develop a focus on a particular aspect of aging. Students will work with the directors to develop a curriculum that best meets their interests and career goals. Students completing the minor will have a basic understanding of the demography of aging, life course development, and policy issues relevant to older adults. This basic understanding provides a strong foundation for students who plan to pursue a career that involves working with older adults or who have a personal interest in understanding aging.

The Global Asia minor introduces students to the study of modern Asia (East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia) as a dynamic and interconnected region of the world. Students in the minor gain a nuanced understanding of Asia’s rich and diverse histories, cultures, and political economies as well as the historical and contemporary flows of people, goods, and ideas that connect Asia with other parts of the world. The minor has an expansive intellectual vision that encourages students to think about Asia from a variety of disciplinary and methodological perspectives. The minor is administered by the Department of Asian Studies, but it is open to all Cornell undergraduates. It is an ideal course of study for students who want to develop an intellectual focus on Asia in addition to their major and for students who want to develop regional expertise for their future careers.

The Global Health Minor is an undergraduate program for students interested in learning about the complex social, economic, political, environmental, and cultural dimensions of health and disease. The minor is open to students from all Cornell colleges. The program is an academic, educational minor, and is not a pre-medical or pre-health program. The program does not grant a professional certificate or license.

The Great Books Minor provides a structured way for students to engage with some of the most influential works of the Western tradition. It invites students to reflect on the meaning of tradition, canonicity, and “greatness” itself. The purpose of the Minor is to encourage students to read important and challenging books in a variety of fields and to do so in a structured, thoughtful, and interdisciplinary way.

We are living in a time of unprecedented specialization, and so it is more important than ever to have a general and well-rounded education. The Great Books Minor offers such an opportunity. It is a supplement, not a rival, to a student’s major. The Minor works particularly well with majors from all the colleges. It allows students a way to make their Cornell education more coherent, more thoughtful, and more integrated.

The Healthy Futures minor is an interdisciplinary undergraduate minor that provides students with a solid foundation to understand and address pressing challenges and opportunities in population health. The minor offers a cohesive curriculum for students who wish to learn about the complex interplay of factors that influence population health locally and globally. It will prepare students to approach health issues from multiple disciplinary perspectives and work with diverse teams to develop solutions for a healthier world.

Students will learn to think critically about the social, environmental, ethical, and policy contexts of population health. They will also gain a foundational understanding of the biological and behavioral determinants of health, and the analytic tools used to evaluate health and health disparities. With a focus on experiential learning, the minor also offers opportunities for students to connect their academic coursework with health related problems and issues in the real-world.

The Hebrew minor, offered by the Department of Near Eastern Studies in the College of Arts and Sciences, helps students to attain a high level of proficiency in all language skills, as well as to become acquainted with the culture (literature, history, religion, politics, etc.) of which the language is a part. Students choosing this minor will have an excellent opportunity to focus their studies on Hebrew and acquire deep knowledge of the specific area that interests them.

The history minor consists of any five history courses, with the following stipulations: at least one course must be in U.S. history; at least one course must be in the history of a country or region other than the U.S. or Europe; at least one course must be in pre-modern history (before 1800); at least one course must be a 4000-level seminar. Cornell in Washington courses and one First-Year Writing Seminar taught by a member of the History Department may be used to fulfill the requirements of the minor. Transfer students may apply up to two history courses from their previous institution toward the minor with the approval of the Director of Undergraduate Studies.

The minor in history of art provides an introduction to the history of art and a deeper grounding in a particular area of interest. It is a good option for students who discover the history of art late in their Cornell careers or for those who want to devote the bulk of their undergraduate coursework to a different field but still maintain a connection to the study of art and its history.

The Horticulture minor is intended for students whose primary academic interests lie in other fields. The minor provides students with a way to organize a series of related courses that can provide a foundation in the science and art of horticulture. The School of Integrative Plant Science offers more than 50 courses in horticulture appropriate for both majors and non-majors.

The Human Development minor provides a structured opportunity for students majoring in other areas to gain a basic foundation in the theories, research findings, and methods of human development from a truly interdisciplinary perspective. The field of human development focuses on how people develop over the entire lifespan in their social, cultural, and historical contexts. As such, the study of human development integrates theory and research from a range of disciplines, including psychology, sociology, biology, and neuroscience. The minor provides a strong background for students considering a wide range of careers including medicine, law, public policy, social work, education, and business.

The Inequality Studies Minor, housed in the Center for the Study of Inequality, is an interdisciplinary program designed for students interested in the systematic study of social and economic inequality. The minor is open to students in all Cornell undergraduate colleges. The curriculum is structured to provide students with a broad understanding of the causes and consequences of inequality, as well as the social, economic, and political responses to it. The minor introduces students to the core subject matter of inequality studies; exposes them to a wide range of analytical and methodological approaches; and deepens their understanding of a particular substantive area of inequality studies.

The minor in Infectious Disease Biology provides an interdisciplinary program of study for students interested in infectious diseases of public health importance, including those that are zoonotic (transmitted from animals to humans) and food-borne. Students take foundational courses in biology and microbiology and then elect further courses in a variety of disciplines including entomology, food science, microbiology, immunology, and animal science. The course of study is designed to provide students with a strong background in the biology of infectious agents and their hosts and with an appreciation of the complex factors that influence the transmission and maintenance of disease-causing agents in a population. Students also gain a broader perspective through the study of socioeconomic and policy factors that are critical to the prevention and control of infectious diseases.

The Information Science Minor provides a coherent program of study in the emerging interdisciplinary field of Information Science. The minor is available to all undergraduate students in all colleges at Cornell. The minor requires the student to complete a core of three courses in Information Science and a set of three electives from an approved list. These electives must form a coherent plan of study, approved by an Information Science faculty advisor.

The minor in International Development (ID) offers a coherent academic focus for undergraduates interested in the challenges of development in low-income countries. The complexity of these issues requires an interdisciplinary approach that encompasses the natural and social sciences. Students are expected to acquire a broad-based knowledge of development issues from a cross-disciplinary perspective and at the same time focus on one particular area in greater depth. The minor is intended to expand students’ understanding of the problems of international development and how they might be addressed.

Concentration name: International Political Economy, International Law and Organizations, Foreign Policy and Diplomatic History, International and Comparative Politics, Culture, Transnationalism, and Globalization
description: The minor in international relations (IR) provides an interdisciplinary program in the study of global affairs. It is designed for students with career and vocational interests in international affairs, including international development and humanitarian assistance, international law and diplomacy, international business and finance, and international security. The minor introduces students to the crucial issues of our time–from global climate change to poverty, trade, and war and peace. The IR minor is not an independent major, but it can be taken in conjunction with any Cornell major. It is housed in the Government Department, but it is open to all students, regardless of college or major.

The minor in International Trade and Development provides students with a framework for understanding the economic relationships among countries, the-institutions that govern these relationships, and the role of trade and other economic policies in promoting development and alleviating poverty.

The Italian studies minor (which is administered by the Department of Romance Studies) is designed to give students a broad understanding of Italian culture. In addition to a solid linguistic foundation, the minor offers an introduction to the rich and diverse cultural production of Italy from the Middle Ages to the present day. It represents a flexible program that can be easily combined with a variety of majors in the humanities, social sciences, and sciences.

The Jewish Studies Minor offers an interdisciplinary approach to the study of Jewish culture, history, and literature from antiquity to the present. The minor is open to students in all colleges of the university.

The minor consists of five courses for a total of at least 20 credits, chosen from the Jewish studies course list. Of the five required courses:

1. Two must be from the following core courses: JWST 1500, JWST 1700/NES 1700, JWST 2644/NES 2644, and JWST 2720/NES 2720.
2. One course must be at the 3000- or 4000-level.
3. One course must be in the pre-modern period, and one in the modern period (a single course may not be used to fulfill both requirements).
4. A single course can be used to fulfill up to two requirements (e.g., JWST 2644 can fulfill both a core course and a pre-modern requirement).
5. One of the courses must be chosen from the approved list of Jewish Studies courses and can be counted towards the student’s major. The other four courses must be taken outside the student’s major or in a different department from the major (in the case of interdisciplinary majors, this means the four courses must not be cross-listed with any other courses counting towards the major). This requirement may be waived at the discretion of the director of undergraduate studies.
6. All courses for the minor must be taken for a letter grade.

All courses to be used for the minor must be approved in writing by the director of undergraduate studies.

The minor in landscape studies is intended for undergraduates who want to become more knowledgeable about the history, theory, and practice of landscape design and land-use planning. The landscape is a dynamic medium that records and expresses natural and cultural processes, and it reflects our values and attitudes toward the environment and toward the land itself. Landscape studies may therefore range in scale from a garden to a continent. The minor offers both a descriptive and a normative view of landscapes, and in a creative and intellectual manner, it encourages students to critically examine issues of nature, design, culture, and place. It also enables students to better understand the ways in which human beings have created and managed the landscapes we inhabit. The minor is offered by the Department of Landscape Architecture in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

The Latin American and Caribbean Studies (LACS) Program offers a university-wide undergraduate minor in Latin American and Caribbean Studies. The LACS minor is designed for students in any of the seven Cornell undergraduate colleges who have a special interest in the region. The LACS minor provides a structured, yet flexible, way to study Latin America and the Caribbean from a variety of disciplinary perspectives. The minor is especially suitable for students who anticipate a career in which a knowledge of the region and its languages is a significant asset. It allows students to focus some of their elective coursework on a fascinating and important part of the world, and to be recognized for it. The minor also helps students prepare for graduate study in Latin American and Caribbean Studies or other international fields.

The Latina/o Studies Program (LSP) Minor is an interdisciplinary program that provides students with a scholarly foundation in the study of Latina/o history, culture, and experience. The minor allows for an in-depth study of the historical trajectories and contemporary lives of Latina/os in the United States and their diasporic communities throughout the Americas. Through a range of courses in the humanities and social sciences, the curriculum examines topics such as racialization, immigration, colonialism, expressive cultures, language, and gender and sexuality.

The Law and Society minor is an interdisciplinary program that allows students to develop a rich, integrated understanding of the social, political, economic, and cultural functions of law. Law and Society scholars use the methods of the social sciences and humanities to study law as a social institution.

The Law and Society minor gives students a framework for understanding legal institutions, rules, and processes, and their relationship to social and historical contexts. It also provides a strong foundation for students considering law school or other graduate programs, as well as those interested in careers in public service, policy, and other law-related professions.

The Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) Studies minor provides an interdisciplinary and scholarly framework for the study of sexuality. Drawing on disciplines in the humanities and social sciences, as well as the natural sciences, the minor in LGBT Studies examines the history, the social and political life, and the creative expressions of lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender people. Courses in the minor analyze the formation of sexual identities; the role of sexuality in the arts, in the media, in science, and in the law; the closet and its consequences; the intersections of sexuality, race, class, and gender; the lives of sexual minorities in the United States and in other cultures; and the achievements of LGBT civil rights movements. Students with a minor in LGBT Studies will be able to apply the critical thinking, reading, writing, and analytical skills fostered by a liberal arts education to a specific and developing field of knowledge. Students minoring in LGBT Studies are required to take one core course, LGBT 2290 - Introduction to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender Studies, and four additional courses from the list of LGBT Studies courses in the catalog. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C or better must be received in all minor courses. Courses are selected by the student in consultation with their LGBT Studies faculty advisor. The advisor is chosen by the student from the list of LGBT Studies faculty.
Program name: Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, & Transgender Studies Minor

description: The linguistics minor provides a systematic introduction to the study of human language. Its core consists of three courses that together provide an overview of the main subfields of the discipline: phonology (the study of speech sounds), syntax (the study of sentence structure), and either semantics (the study of meaning) or historical linguistics (the study of language change and the history and development of languages). Further courses may be chosen according to a student’s own interests, and may focus on a variety of topics, including the language of a particular geographical area, computational linguistics, language and society, and animal communication. An understanding of linguistics is highly relevant to students with an interest in human cognition (psychology, philosophy, anthropology), in literature and the humanities, in computer science, and in the study of specific foreign languages. Students minoring in linguistics are encouraged to take courses in a variety of languages, since an appreciation of the diversity of human language is central to the field. Many courses in various language departments may be used to satisfy some of the requirements for the minor. Students should select these courses in consultation with their minor advisor, to ensure a coherent program of study that familiarizes them with the different ways in which human languages can vary, as well as in more distantly related languages.

The Materials Science and Engineering (MSE) minor provides a coherent program of study for students who want a strong background in materials science and engineering but are majoring in another field. The minor requires a minimum of six courses. Three of these must be from the MSE Core Curriculum: MSE 2610, MSE 2620, and MSE 3010. Two more must be chosen from a specific list of MSE senior-level courses. The final requirement is one additional MSE course that is not a special-project course. All courses must be taken for a letter grade and a grade of C- or better must be achieved in each course.

The Mathematics Minor is designed to give students a strong background in mathematics, which is useful for graduate study in many fields. Students considering the Mathematics Minor should consult a faculty member in the Department of Mathematics. To be admitted to the minor, students should complete the application form available at the department office or on the department website. Students must complete all minor requirements by their graduation date. In some cases, courses may be used to satisfy requirements for both a major and a minor.

The Mechanical Engineering minor is intended for students who are not majoring in mechanical engineering but who are interested in the field. The minor provides students with an introduction to the core areas of mechanical engineering, including mechanics, materials, thermal sciences, and design. The minor is flexible, allowing students to tailor their course selection to their specific interests.

The undergraduate minor in Media Studies, housed in the Department of Performing and Media Arts, is an interdisciplinary program that includes courses in a wide variety of departments. The minor offers students the opportunity to study the history, theory, and practice of a wide range of media forms. Students learn to think critically about media as cultural and aesthetic forms that are linked to particular social, political, and economic contexts. The minor aims to provide students with a broad understanding of different media (print, radio, film, television, video, digital media) and to familiarize them with a range of analytical and theoretical approaches to media studies. The interdisciplinary nature of the minor encourages students to consider media from multiple perspectives and to develop a comparative framework for their study.

The undergraduate minor in Medieval Studies is a multidisciplinary program that offers a coherent and comprehensive, yet flexible, program for students who wish to pursue a special interest in the culture of the Middle Ages. The minor can attractively supplement a major in such fields as classics, history, languages and literatures, philosophy, or religious studies. The requirements for the minor are sufficiently flexible to accommodate a wide variety of interests and needs—from the student who is just beginning to explore a new field to the one who is already planning graduate work in a medieval specialization. Each student’s program is planned in consultation with the Director of Undergraduate Studies, with whom all interested students are urged to discuss their plans. Students complete five courses from a variety of offerings in Art History, Classics, Comparative Literature, English, German Studies, History, Music, Near Eastern Studies, Philosophy, Religious Studies, and Romance Studies.

The Minor in Microbiology is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the roles that microorganisms play in the natural world and in human affairs. The minor provides a strong foundation in the fundamental principles of microbiology, including microbial physiology, genetics, and diversity, as well as opportunities for more specialized study in areas such as microbial pathogenesis, environmental microbiology, and biotechnology. Students in the minor will also develop practical skills in laboratory techniques and data analysis. The minor prepares students for a variety of careers in fields such as medicine, public health, biotechnology, and environmental science, as well as for advanced study in microbiology and related disciplines.

The undergraduate minor in migration studies, open to students in all Cornell undergraduate colleges, provides a framework for students to pursue a comprehensive, interdisciplinary course of study of migration. The core courses of the minor provide a firm grounding in the historical, political, economic, social and cultural dimensions of migration and its consequences. From that base, students build an individualized course of study, drawing from a rich menu of migration-related courses taught by faculty from across the university and relevant off-campus study programs. The minor is administered by the Migrations initiative.

The Minority, Indigenous, and Third World Studies (MITWS) undergraduate minor, housed in the Cornell Center for Social Sciences, is a LSA-affiliated program that offers an interdisciplinary curriculum to students interested in the histories, cultures, and socioeconomic and political conditions of marginalized and subaltern peoples in the U.S. and around the world. The curriculum in MITWS places a strong emphasis on the politics of race, ethnicity, indigeneity, and diaspora. By taking a comparative and global approach to the study of social marginalization, the MITWS minor encourages students to critically examine the production and articulation of racial and ethnic identities, and the structural and institutional bases of inequality and oppression. The curriculum for the minor is designed to provide students with the critical and analytical tools to engage with a variety of social and cultural issues, including racial and ethnic formations, indigenous sovereignty and rights, migration and displacement, colonialism and post-colonialism, and social justice and human rights. Students pursuing the minor must complete an introductory course, four elective courses and a senior seminar. Students are encouraged to consult with the MITWS faculty in designing a curriculum that is tailored to their specific intellectual interests, and in choosing an advisor for the senior seminar paper. For the most up to date information and course listings, see the program website at lsp.cornell.edu/minority-indigenous-and-third-world-studies, or contact the Program Manager as well as the MITWS Program Director.
Program name: Minority, Indigenous, and Third World Studies Minor

description: The minor in Near Eastern studies is designed to provide undergraduate students with a general knowledge and understanding of the cultures, civilizations, languages, and literatures of the Near East from antiquity to the modern day. The minor is sufficiently flexible to accommodate a wide variety of student interests and to be easily combined with a number of different majors.
